5. The likelihood of a dependent record

IN THIS CHAPTER

  1. 5.1 State what is observed and what is unknown
  2. 5.2 Derive the product rule from the definition of conditional probability
  3. 5.3 Build the chain rule for three and then many observations
  4. 5.4 Now use the Markov assumption—and only now
  5. 5.5 Work through one fully specified discrete record
  6. 5.6 Endpoint probability versus observed-record probability
  7. 5.7 Move from masses to densities without changing the structure
  8. 5.8 A continuous example with every likelihood factor visible
  9. 5.9 Conditional likelihood does not discard the starting value
  10. 5.10 Derive a two-state chain MLE from transition counts
  11. 5.11 The logarithm changes computation, not the probability model

5.1 State what is observed and what is unknown

Suppose you observe a process at n+1n+1 successive recording times and obtain the numerical record

D=(x0,x1,…,xn). D=(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n).

The corresponding uncertain values before observation are X0,X1,…,XnX_0,X_1,\ldots,X_n. A parameter vector η\eta specifies the model’s transition probabilities or densities. The actual parameter vector is unknown; for likelihood evaluation, we insert candidate values of η\eta and calculate how well each candidate assigns probability or density to this fixed record.

For an independent coin sample, the likelihood is a product of individual probabilities. For a process, the values are typically dependent. Today’s position helps predict tomorrow’s position. Multiplying the individual marginal probabilities Pη(Xi=xi)P_\eta(X_i=x_i) would ignore that structure.

We need a factorization that remains valid for dependent observations. The tool is the probability chain rule. The Markov property will simplify the chain rule, but the two ideas must be introduced separately.

5.2 Derive the product rule from the definition of conditional probability

For events AA and BB with P(A)>0P(A)>0, conditional probability is

P(B∣A)=P(A∩B)P(A). P(B\mid A)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)}.

Multiplying by P(A)P(A) gives

P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B∣A). P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B\mid A).

This is an identity. It does not require independence. If AA and BB happen to be independent, then P(B∣A)=P(B)P(B\mid A)=P(B) and the formula reduces to P(A)P(B)P(A)P(B). Without independence, the conditional factor must be retained.

The same identity works inside a world where another event CC is already supplied:

P(A∩B∣C)=P(A∣C)P(B∣A,C). P(A\cap B\mid C)=P(A\mid C)P(B\mid A,C).

You can verify it by inserting the definitions and canceling denominators. Supplying a model parameter does not change this algebra; every probability is simply evaluated under the same candidate probability law PηP_\eta.

5.3 Build the chain rule for three and then many observations

Begin with three observations. Apply the product rule to the block (X0,X1)(X_0,X_1) and the final value X2X_2:

Pη(X0=x0,X1=x1,X2=x2)=Pη(X0=x0,X1=x1)Pη(X2=x2∣X0=x0,X1=x1). \begin{aligned} &P_\eta(X_0=x_0,X_1=x_1,X_2=x_2)\\ &\quad=P_\eta(X_0=x_0,X_1=x_1) P_\eta(X_2=x_2\mid X_0=x_0,X_1=x_1). \end{aligned}

Apply it again to the first block:

Pη(X0=x0,X1=x1,X2=x2)=Pη(X0=x0)Pη(X1=x1∣X0=x0)×Pη(X2=x2∣X0=x0,X1=x1). \begin{aligned} &P_\eta(X_0=x_0,X_1=x_1,X_2=x_2)\\ &=P_\eta(X_0=x_0) P_\eta(X_1=x_1\mid X_0=x_0)\\ &\qquad\times P_\eta(X_2=x_2\mid X_0=x_0,X_1=x_1). \end{aligned}

Each new factor asks for the next observation conditional on everything preceding it. Continuing in this way gives

Pη(X0=x0,…,Xn=xn)=Pη(X0=x0)∏i=1nPη(Xi=xi∣X0=x0,…,Xi−1=xi−1). \boxed{ P_\eta(X_0=x_0,\ldots,X_n=x_n) =P_\eta(X_0=x_0) \prod_{i=1}^n P_\eta(X_i=x_i\mid X_0=x_0,\ldots,X_{i-1}=x_{i-1}). }

For compactness we will sometimes write this as

pη(x0,…,xn)=pη(x0)∏i=1npη(xi∣x0,…,xi−1). p_\eta(x_0,\ldots,x_n) =p_\eta(x_0)\prod_{i=1}^n p_\eta(x_i\mid x_0,\ldots,x_{i-1}).

The lowercase pηp_\eta here denotes a mass function, not the coin’s single scalar heads probability. Its arguments identify what distribution it describes.

The important fact is that the chain rule is always available when the relevant conditional laws are defined. It does not make a process Markov. It simply writes a joint probability as a sequence of conditional probabilities.

5.4 Now use the Markov assumption—and only now

A first-order Markov model says that the conditional law of the next state given its entire past equals its conditional law given only its immediately preceding state:

pη(xi∣x0,…,xi−1)=pη(xi∣xi−1). p_\eta(x_i\mid x_0,\ldots,x_{i-1}) =p_\eta(x_i\mid x_{i-1}).

Substitute that equality into each conditional factor of the chain rule:

pη(x0,…,xn)=pη(x0)∏i=1npη(xi∣xi−1). \boxed{ p_\eta(x_0,\ldots,x_n) =p_\eta(x_0)\prod_{i=1}^n p_\eta(x_i\mid x_{i-1}). }

The observations have not become independent. Each factor still depends on the previous observed state. What has disappeared is the need to carry every older observation as a conditioning argument.

This separates the two mathematical ingredients cleanly. The chain rule justifies multiplication. The Markov property shortens the history in each conditional. Neither can be replaced by the vague explanation that “the observations are independent.”

5.5 Work through one fully specified discrete record

Use a two-state homogeneous chain with

p11=0.7,p12=0.3,p21=0.4,p22=0.6, p_{11}=0.7,\quad p_{12}=0.3,\quad p_{21}=0.4,\quad p_{22}=0.6,

where pijp_{ij} is the probability of moving from state ii to state jj. Suppose the observed record is (1,1,2,1)(1,1,2,1) and the initial distribution assigns probability 1/21/2 to state 11.

The record contains the three observed transitions 1→11\to1, 1→21\to2, and 2→12\to1. Its full probability is

P(X0=1,X1=1,X2=2,X3=1)=P(X0=1)p11p12p21=12(0.7)(0.3)(0.4)=0.042. \begin{aligned} P(X_0=1,X_1=1,X_2=2,X_3=1) &=P(X_0=1)p_{11}p_{12}p_{21}\\ &=\tfrac12(0.7)(0.3)(0.4)\\ &=0.042. \end{aligned}

If the starting state is supplied as a condition rather than modeled as random, then

P(X1=1,X2=2,X3=1∣X0=1)=(0.7)(0.3)(0.4)=0.084. P(X_1=1,X_2=2,X_3=1\mid X_0=1) =(0.7)(0.3)(0.4)=0.084.

The first calculation asks for the probability of the start and the subsequent record. The second asks for the probability of the subsequent record given that start. They are different questions, so different numerical answers are appropriate.

5.6 Endpoint probability versus observed-record probability

Suppose instead that you observe only X0=1X_0=1 and X2=1X_2=1, with the middle state unobserved. There are two possible routes: (1,1,1)(1,1,1) and (1,2,1)(1,2,1). The conditional endpoint probability is

P(X2=1∣X0=1)=p112+p12p21=0.49+0.12=0.61. P(X_2=1\mid X_0=1)=p_{11}^2+p_{12}p_{21}=0.49+0.12=0.61.

If the full route (1,1,1)(1,1,1) was observed, its conditional probability would be only p112=0.49p_{11}^2=0.49. We would not add the other route because it did not occur in the recorded data.

The rule is: sum over unobserved alternatives; retain observed intermediate values in the product. Matrix powers perform these route sums for finite homogeneous chains. A continuous-state transition over a long interval likewise already accounts for all unobserved behavior within that interval; one should not invent unobserved intermediate observations and multiply their densities into a likelihood.

A useful related question is reconstruction of the missing middle state. Take a weather chain with S→S=0.8S\to S=0.8, S→R=0.2S\to R=0.2, R→S=0.4R\to S=0.4, and R→R=0.6R\to R=0.6. Given SS at time zero and RR at time two, the chance of rain at the middle time is

P(R1∣S0,R2)=P(R1,R2∣S0)P(R2∣S0)=0.2(0.6)0.8(0.2)+0.2(0.6)=0.120.28=37. \begin{aligned} P(R_1\mid S_0,R_2) &=\frac{P(R_1,R_2\mid S_0)}{P(R_2\mid S_0)}\\ &=\frac{0.2(0.6)}{0.8(0.2)+0.2(0.6)}\\ &=\frac{0.12}{0.28}=\frac37. \end{aligned}

The numerator is the one route consistent with a rainy middle state. The denominator is the sum of all routes consistent with the observations. Every factor has a specific conditioning interpretation.

5.7 Move from masses to densities without changing the structure

For continuous observations, the exact-value probability P(Xi=xi)P(X_i=x_i) is zero. The probability of a small interval is obtained by integrating a density over that interval. Therefore likelihood uses a joint density evaluated at the recorded values, not the probability of the exact-value event.

The density version of conditional probability is

fη(x,y)=fη(x)fη(y∣x), f_\eta(x,y)=f_\eta(x)f_\eta(y\mid x),

where a conditional density can be obtained by the ratio fη(x,y)/fη(x)f_\eta(x,y)/f_\eta(x) wherever the denominator is positive. Repeating the identity gives the same chain factorization. For a Markov process with initial density hηh_\eta and transition density gηg_\eta,

fη(x0,…,xn)=hη(x0)∏i=1ngη(xi∣xi−1). \boxed{ f_\eta(x_0,\ldots,x_n) =h_\eta(x_0)\prod_{i=1}^n g_\eta(x_i\mid x_{i-1}). }

For each fixed current state xx, the function y↦gη(y∣x)y\mapsto g_\eta(y\mid x) is a full probability density over the next state: it is nonnegative and integrates to one. At the observed next value yy, its height supplies the transition’s likelihood contribution.

If the transition depends on an elapsed time Δi\Delta_i, write gη(xi∣xi−1;Δi)g_\eta(x_i\mid x_{i-1};\Delta_i). The time gap is observed information controlling the transition, not an extra unknown parameter unless a separate sampling model is being estimated. We will work through this explicitly for OU observations in Chapter 13.

5.8 A continuous example with every likelihood factor visible

Consider the recursion

Xi=25+0.5(Xi−1−25)+εi,εi∼N(0,4), X_i=25+0.5(X_{i-1}-25)+\varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i\sim N(0,4),

where the innovations εi\varepsilon_i are mutually independent and independent of the starting value. The notation N(m,v)N(m,v) means a Gaussian distribution with mean mm and variance vv.

Given Xi−1=xX_{i-1}=x, the only remaining random quantity is εi\varepsilon_i. Therefore

Xi∣Xi−1=x∼N(25+0.5(x−25),4). X_i\mid X_{i-1}=x\sim N\bigl(25+0.5(x-25),4\bigr).

The corresponding transition density is

g(y∣x)=18πexp[−(y−25−0.5(x−25))28]. g(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8\pi}} \exp\left[-\frac{(y-25-0.5(x-25))^2}{8}\right].

Now observe (x0,x1,x2)=(29,27,25.5)(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(29,27,25.5) and condition on x0=29x_0=29. For the first transition, the predicted mean is 25+0.5(29−25)=2725+0.5(29-25)=27, so the observed error is zero. The factor is g(27∣29)=1/8πg(27\mid29)=1/\sqrt{8\pi}.

For the second transition, the observed current value is 2727, not an unobserved prediction. The predicted next mean is 25+0.5(27−25)=2625+0.5(27-25)=26. The actual next observation is 25.525.5, so the error is −0.5-0.5 and its square is 0.250.25. Thus

g(25.5∣27)=18πexp[−0.258]. g(25.5\mid27)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8\pi}}\exp\left[-\frac{0.25}{8}\right].

Multiply the two factors:

L=18πe−1/32. \boxed{L=\frac{1}{8\pi}e^{-1/32}.}

This is a joint conditional density value, not a dimensionless probability of those exact real numbers. In this calculation the parameters were fixed at (25,0.5,4)(25,0.5,4) simply to evaluate a candidate. For estimation, replace them by (μ,ϕ,τ2)(\mu,\phi,\tau^2), keep (29,27,25.5)(29,27,25.5) fixed, and maximize the resulting function of the candidate parameters.

5.9 Conditional likelihood does not discard the starting value

The conditional likelihood is

Lc(η)=∏i=1ngη(xi∣xi−1). L_c(\eta)=\prod_{i=1}^n g_\eta(x_i\mid x_{i-1}).

The full likelihood is

Lf(η)=hη(x0)Lc(η). L_f(\eta)=h_\eta(x_0)L_c(\eta).

Notice that x0x_0 is still used in the first conditional transition of LcL_c. Conditioning removes the density factor for how the start was generated, not the start’s numerical role in predicting x1x_1.

There are several legitimate setups. If the initial value was fixed by experimental design, no initial random density is needed. If it was drawn from a known distribution independent of η\eta, its density factor is constant with respect to the optimization and does not alter the maximizing parameter. If it was drawn from a stationary distribution depending on η\eta, that factor generally changes the full likelihood and may change the estimate.

The fact that x0x_0 is observed does not make hη(x0)h_\eta(x_0) constant in η\eta. All observations in a likelihood are observed and fixed; their probabilities or densities still vary across candidate models. This is exactly the data-versus-parameter distinction from the coin example.

“Exact transition likelihood” and “full likelihood” also answer different questions. A conditional likelihood can use exact transitions. A full likelihood additionally specifies the initial law. Neither word should silently stand in for the other.

5.10 Derive a two-state chain MLE from transition counts

Let a=p11a=p_{11} and b=p21b=p_{21} be unknown. Then p12=1−ap_{12}=1-a and p22=1−bp_{22}=1-b. The unknown parameter vector is (a,b)(a,b); the observed data are a state sequence. Condition on its start.

Use the concrete record

1,1,2,1,2,2,1,1,1,2,1. 1,1,2,1,2,2,1,1,1,2,1.

It contains ten transitions. Counting them gives n11=3n_{11}=3, n12=3n_{12}=3, n21=3n_{21}=3, and n22=1n_{22}=1. Each 1→11\to1 contributes aa, each 1→21\to2 contributes 1−a1-a, and so on. Consequently,

Lc(a,b)=a3(1−a)3b3(1−b). L_c(a,b)=a^3(1-a)^3 b^3(1-b).

Taking logs produces

ℓ(a,b)=3loga+3log(1−a)+3logb+log(1−b). \ell(a,b)=3\log a+3\log(1-a)+3\log b+\log(1-b).

The terms involving aa and bb are separate. Differentiating with respect to aa while holding bb fixed gives

3a−31−a=0⇒â=36=12. \frac3a-\frac3{1-a}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat a=\frac36=\frac12.

Differentiating in bb gives

3b−11−b=0⇒b̂=34. \frac3b-\frac1{1-b}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat b=\frac34.

Both second derivatives are negative in the interior, so the solutions maximize their respective blocks. The estimate of an outgoing transition probability is the number of observed departures of that type divided by the total number of observed departures from the same state.

For a general finite chain, this yields

p̂ij=nij∑knik, \hat p_{ij}=\frac{n_{ij}}{\sum_k n_{ik}},

provided the denominator is positive. If no departure from state ii is observed, the conditional likelihood contains no factor involving its outgoing distribution, so that distribution is not identified by these data. It is incorrect to manufacture an estimate by dividing zero by zero.

The transition counts summarize the dependence of this conditional likelihood on the parameters. This is the relevant meaning of a sufficient statistic here. It does not mean that the observed transitions are i.i.d., or that any arbitrary array of counts can come from one path. For example, in a two-state path the difference n12−n21n_{12}-n_{21} can only be −1-1, 00, or 11, depending on the starting and ending states. Our concrete record obeys that constraint.

5.11 The logarithm changes computation, not the probability model

For the general Markov likelihood,

ℓf(η)=loghη(x0)+∑i=1nloggη(xi∣xi−1). \ell_f(\eta)=\log h_\eta(x_0)+\sum_{i=1}^n\log g_\eta(x_i\mid x_{i-1}).

Taking logs converts a product of many factors into a sum. It does not remove dependence, justify a Markov assumption, or change the initial-condition decision. Those were modeling choices made before the logarithm was taken.

The advantage is that each recorded transition contributes one evaluable term. A long record does not force the conditioning history of each term to grow, provided the process is truly Markov in the recorded state. If the state is incomplete, such as a noisy measurement of an unobserved Markov state, the recorded series need not inherit this simple factorization using the latent state’s transition density. A different observation model may be needed.

The Gaussian AR(1) model supplies a concrete transition density for which this likelihood can be derived and optimized by hand. That is the subject of the next two chapters.

Source connection: MIT Lecture 5 supplies the Markov framework, and MIT Lecture 8 discusses time-series likelihoods. Every factorization and numerical example above is developed from the stated conditional laws.

6. Give the process a home

IN THIS CHAPTER

  2. 6.2 Conditional prediction: what stays fixed and what remains random

  4. 6.4 Why the model is Markov

  6. 6.6 Derive the finite-time mean

6.1 What a random walk cannot express

A random walk evolves as Wi+1=Wi+Si+1W_{i+1}=W_i+S_{i+1}, where Si+1S_{i+1} is a fresh independent step. If the step mean is zero, knowing Wi=wW_i=w gives expected next position ww. The process has no preferred level. An unusually high current position does not, by itself, create a downward expected correction.

Now imagine a quantity that tends to return toward a normal level, while still receiving unpredictable disturbances. To model that behavior, specify a target level μ\mu and retain only a fraction ϕ\phi of the current deviation from it. Then add new noise:

Xi=μ+ϕ(Xi−1−μ)+εi. \boxed{X_i=\mu+\phi(X_{i-1}-\mu)+\varepsilon_i.}

For this chapter, initially treat the parameters as known. We want to understand the model’s behavior. Estimating the parameters from observations is a separate problem, treated in Chapter 7.

The quantity XiX_i is the state at tick ii. The parameter μ\mu is the level toward which the conditional mean tends. The coefficient ϕ\phi is the fraction of a deviation retained for one tick. The random innovation εi\varepsilon_i is the fresh unpredictable contribution at that tick. We assume

εi∼N(0,τ2),τ2>0, \varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\tau^2),\qquad \tau^2>0,

with all innovations mutually independent and independent of the initial value X0X_0. The notation N(m,v)N(m,v) means Gaussian with mean mm and variance vv. Thus τ\tau is the innovation standard deviation, and τ2\tau^2 is its variance.

“Autoregressive of order one,” abbreviated AR(1), means that the next value is expressed using one lag of the same process. Rewriting the equation gives the familiar intercept-and-slope form

Xi=μ(1−ϕ)⏟intercept+ϕXi−1+εi. X_i=\underbrace{\mu(1-\phi)}_{\text{intercept}}+\phi X_{i-1}+\varepsilon_i.

6.2 Conditional prediction: what stays fixed and what remains random

Suppose the current value is observed as Xi−1=xX_{i-1}=x. Under this condition, the quantity μ+ϕ(x−μ)\mu+\phi(x-\mu) is a fixed number. The only remaining uncertainty in the next value is the innovation. Adding a constant to a Gaussian shifts its mean and leaves its variance unchanged. Therefore

Xi∣Xi−1=x∼N(μ+ϕ(x−μ),τ2). \boxed{X_i\mid X_{i-1}=x\sim N\bigl(\mu+\phi(x-\mu),\tau^2\bigr).}

Conditional expectation averages over the remaining randomness while holding the supplied current value fixed. Since E[εi]=0E[\varepsilon_i]=0,

E[Xi∣Xi−1=x]=μ+ϕ(x−μ). E[X_i\mid X_{i-1}=x]=\mu+\phi(x-\mu).

Conditional variance measures the uncertainty around that prediction. Because the predictable part is constant under the condition,

Var(Xi∣Xi−1=x)=τ2. \operatorname{Var}(X_i\mid X_{i-1}=x)=\tau^2.

Take μ=25\mu=25, ϕ=1/2\phi=1/2, and τ2=4\tau^2=4. If the current observation is 2929, then the deviation is 29−25=429-25=4. Half remains in the forecast, giving predicted next value 25+2=2725+2=27. The distribution is N(27,4)N(27,4), with standard deviation 22.

If the realized innovation is −1-1, the next value is 2626. If it is 33, the next value is 3030. Both are compatible with the same mean-reverting model. In fact,

P(Xi>29∣Xi−1=29)=P(Z>29−272)=P(Z>1), P(X_i>29\mid X_{i-1}=29) =P\left(Z>\frac{29-27}{2}\right)=P(Z>1),

where Z∼N(0,1)Z\sim N(0,1). This probability is about 0.1590.159. Mean reversion does not prohibit an upward move from an already high value. It describes the average conditional move, not every realized move.

6.3 Derive the expected pull toward the target

Subtract the supplied current value xx from the conditional mean:

E[Xi−Xi−1∣Xi−1=x]=μ+ϕ(x−μ)−x=μ−ϕμ+ϕx−x=(1−ϕ)μ−(1−ϕ)x=−(1−ϕ)(x−μ). \begin{aligned} E[X_i-X_{i-1}\mid X_{i-1}=x] &=\mu+\phi(x-\mu)-x\\ &=\mu-\phi\mu+\phi x-x\\ &=(1-\phi)\mu-(1-\phi)x\\ &=-(1-\phi)(x-\mu). \end{aligned}

When 0<ϕ<10<\phi<1, the factor 1−ϕ1-\phi is positive. If x>μx>\mu, the expected change is negative; if x<μx<\mu, it is positive. If x=μx=\mu, there is no expected drift, although noise still produces movement.

For x≠μx\ne\mu and 0<ϕ<10<\phi<1, the conditional mean lies strictly between xx and μ\mu. A smaller positive ϕ\phi means less of the deviation survives one tick, hence faster mean reversion on that tick scale.

The parameter range matters. At ϕ=0\phi=0, the next value is μ+εi\mu+\varepsilon_i and forgets the current value completely. For −1<ϕ<0-1<\phi<0, the conditional deviation changes sign at each tick while its magnitude shrinks: the model oscillates around μ\mu. At ϕ=1\phi=1, the level parameter cancels and the model becomes Xi=Xi−1+εiX_i=X_{i-1}+\varepsilon_i, a Gaussian random walk. At |ϕ|>1|\phi|>1, the deterministic effect of a deviation grows rather than decays.

The stable causal AR(1) model with fresh independent innovations uses |ϕ|<1|\phi|<1. The mean-reverting scalar OU model sampled at a positive fixed time gap corresponds specifically to 0<ϕ<10<\phi<1; it does not produce a negative coefficient of this kind.

6.4 Why the model is Markov

Given the entire history through tick i−1i-1, the new innovation is still independent Gaussian noise. The recursion only uses that history through Xi−1X_{i-1}. Therefore the conditional distribution of XiX_i given X0,…,Xi−1X_0,\ldots,X_{i-1} is the same Gaussian as the one given Xi−1X_{i-1} alone.

This proves the first-order Markov property for the specified model. The argument depends on the fresh-noise assumption. Merely writing a formula with a symbol εi\varepsilon_i would not prove Markovness if the noise retained extra dependence on older states.

The innovations are independent; the states are not. An innovation at an early time is carried forward through the recursion and affects several later states. To see exactly how, we now solve the recursion.

6.5 Unroll the equation instead of skipping to a formula

Center the process at the target by defining Yi=Xi−μY_i=X_i-\mu. Then

Yi=ϕYi−1+εi. Y_i=\phi Y_{i-1}+\varepsilon_i.

Start from a fixed X0=x0X_0=x_0, hence Y0=x0−μY_0=x_0-\mu. The first three expansions are

Y1=ϕY0+ε1, Y_1=\phi Y_0+\varepsilon_1,

Y2=ϕY1+ε2=ϕ(ϕY0+ε1)+ε2=ϕ2Y0+ϕε1+ε2, \begin{aligned} Y_2&=\phi Y_1+\varepsilon_2\\ &=\phi(\phi Y_0+\varepsilon_1)+\varepsilon_2\\ &=\phi^2Y_0+\phi\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2, \end{aligned}

and

Y3=ϕ3Y0+ϕ2ε1+ϕε2+ε3. Y_3=\phi^3Y_0+\phi^2\varepsilon_1+\phi\varepsilon_2+\varepsilon_3.

Every existing contribution is multiplied by ϕ\phi each time it advances one more tick. The newest innovation has multiplier one; an innovation from rr ticks ago has multiplier ϕr\phi^r.

The resulting general expression is

Xk=μ+ϕk(x0−μ)+∑j=1kϕk−jεj. \boxed{X_k=\mu+\phi^k(x_0-\mu)+\sum_{j=1}^k\phi^{k-j}\varepsilon_j.}

It can be checked by induction: multiply the centered expression at tick kk by ϕ\phi, append εk+1\varepsilon_{k+1}, and the formula at tick k+1k+1 follows. Thus the expansion is a solution of the recursion, not just a visual pattern.

6.6 Derive the finite-time mean

The starting deviation is a fixed number, while each innovation has mean zero. Linearity of expectation gives

E[Xk∣X0=x0]=μ+ϕk(x0−μ)+∑j=1kϕk−jE[εj]=μ+ϕk(x0−μ). \begin{aligned} E[X_k\mid X_0=x_0] &=\mu+\phi^k(x_0-\mu)+\sum_{j=1}^k\phi^{k-j}E[\varepsilon_j]\\ &=\mu+\phi^k(x_0-\mu). \end{aligned}

For |ϕ|<1|\phi|<1, the factor ϕk\phi^k tends to zero. Hence the mean approaches μ\mu as the number of ticks grows. That is why μ\mu is called the long-run mean or mean-reversion level.

It is not necessarily the mean at every finite time. Starting at 2929 with μ=25\mu=25 and ϕ=1/2\phi=1/2, the successive means are 2727, 2626, 25.525.5, and so on. Their destination is 2525, but their finite-time values are not all 2525.

6.7 Derive the finite-time variance and the geometric sum

For a fixed start, only the innovation sum contributes variance. If a variable is multiplied by aa, its variance is multiplied by a2a^2, since

E[(aU−E[aU])2]=a2E[(U−E[U])2]. E[(aU-E[aU])^2]=a^2E[(U-E[U])^2].

Distinct innovations are independent, so the covariance terms vanish. Therefore

Var(Xk∣X0=x0)=∑j=1kVar(ϕk−jεj)=τ2∑j=1kϕ2(k−j)=τ2(1+ϕ2+ϕ4+⋯+ϕ2(k−1)). \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(X_k\mid X_0=x_0) &=\sum_{j=1}^k\operatorname{Var}(\phi^{k-j}\varepsilon_j)\\ &=\tau^2\sum_{j=1}^k\phi^{2(k-j)}\\ &=\tau^2(1+\phi^2+\phi^4+\cdots+\phi^{2(k-1)}). \end{aligned}

Let Gk=1+r+⋯+rk−1G_k=1+r+\cdots+r^{k-1}. Then rGk=r+r2+⋯+rkrG_k=r+r^2+\cdots+r^k. Subtracting gives (1−r)Gk=1−rk(1-r)G_k=1-r^k, so Gk=(1−rk)/(1−r)G_k=(1-r^k)/(1-r) for r≠1r\ne1. With r=ϕ2r=\phi^2,

Var(Xk∣X0=x0)=τ21−ϕ2k1−ϕ2,|ϕ|<1. \boxed{\operatorname{Var}(X_k\mid X_0=x_0) =\tau^2\frac{1-\phi^{2k}}{1-\phi^2}},\qquad |\phi|<1.

The square in 1−ϕ21-\phi^2 is essential. It appears because variance squares the innovation weights. Using 1−ϕ1-\phi would be summing the wrong powers.

For the numerical model (μ,ϕ,τ2)=(25,1/2,4)(\mu,\phi,\tau^2)=(25,1/2,4), the first variance is 44. The second is 4(1+1/4)=54(1+1/4)=5. The third is 4(1+1/4+1/16)=5.254(1+1/4+1/16)=5.25. The variance is increasing from a known initial value, but it is approaching a finite limit rather than increasing without bound as in a random walk.

6.8 Why the finite-time law is exactly Gaussian

The expansion is a constant plus a finite weighted sum of independent Gaussian variables. Such a sum is Gaussian. This is an exact closure property, not a central-limit approximation.

One way to justify it is through exponential moments. If U∼N(m,v)U\sim N(m,v), completing the square in its density integral gives

E[erU]=erm+r2v/2. E[e^{rU}]=e^{rm+r^2v/2}.

To see where that Gaussian exponential moment comes from, insert the Gaussian density into the definition of expectation. For v>0v>0,

E[erU]=∫−∞∞eru12πve−(u−m)2/(2v)du. E[e^{rU}]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{ru}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}}e^{-(u-m)^2/(2v)}du.

Complete the square in the exponent:

ru−(u−m)22v=−(u−m−rv)22v+rm+r2v2. ru-\frac{(u-m)^2}{2v} =-\frac{(u-m-rv)^2}{2v}+rm+\frac{r^2v}{2}.

The terms rm+r2v/2rm+r^2v/2 do not involve uu, so their exponential can be taken outside the integral. The remaining integrand is the density of N(m+rv,v)N(m+rv,v), whose integral is 1. This proves the displayed expression for E[erU]E[e^{rU}]. It is a way of describing a distribution through a function of the auxiliary number rr, not an extra model parameter being estimated.

For independent UjU_j, the exponential moment of ∑jajUj\sum_j a_jU_j factors into ∏jE[erajUj]\prod_jE[e^{ra_jU_j}]. Multiplying the expressions above gives

exp[r∑jajmj+r22∑jaj2vj], \exp\left[r\sum_j a_jm_j+\frac{r^2}{2}\sum_j a_j^2v_j\right],

which is the exponential-moment function of a Gaussian with those mean and variance parameters. The standard uniqueness result for such moment-generating functions identifies the distribution. The essential mechanism is independence plus the quadratic form of the Gaussian exponential moment.

Thus, for a fixed initial value,

Xk∣X0=x0∼N(μ+ϕk(x0−μ),τ21−ϕ2k1−ϕ2). X_k\mid X_0=x_0 \sim N\left(\mu+\phi^k(x_0-\mu),\ \tau^2\frac{1-\phi^{2k}}{1-\phi^2}\right).

If the initial value is random and non-Gaussian, an unconditional finite-time state need not be Gaussian. Its distribution contains the transformed initial randomness as well as Gaussian innovations. The conditioning or initialization assumption must accompany the Gaussian claim.

6.9 Stationary variance as a balance of old and new uncertainty

For |ϕ|<1|\phi|<1, the finite-time variance tends to

q=τ21−ϕ2. q=\frac{\tau^2}{1-\phi^2}.

Here qq denotes a stationary state variance, not an innovation variance. The distinction is physical: τ2\tau^2 is new uncertainty injected on one tick; qq includes the surviving contributions of all past innovations.

We can derive the same formula by asking which variance would remain unchanged under a transition. Suppose the current state has variance qq and is independent of the next innovation. The next state has variance ϕ2q+τ2\phi^2q+\tau^2. For it to remain qq, we require

q=ϕ2q+τ2⇒(1−ϕ2)q=τ2⇒q=τ21−ϕ2. q=\phi^2q+\tau^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (1-\phi^2)q=\tau^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q=\frac{\tau^2}{1-\phi^2}.

If the current state is Gaussian with mean μ\mu and variance qq, the next is Gaussian too. Its mean remains μ\mu and its variance remains qq, so the entire one-time distribution is preserved:

π=N(μ,τ21−ϕ2). \boxed{\pi=N\left(\mu,\frac{\tau^2}{1-\phi^2}\right).}

Initialize X0X_0 from this distribution independently of all future innovations. Because the transition rule is the same at every tick, every finite block of states then has a distribution unchanged by a common shift in time. This is a stationary process.

Starting from a fixed x0x_0 produces convergence toward this distribution, not stationarity from the first tick. Also, convergence of distributions does not mean individual paths eventually stop at μ\mu. Fresh noise continues to enter forever.

6.10 Derive autocovariance and autocorrelation

In stationarity, each state has variance qq. To compare states kk ticks apart, restart the expansion at tick ii:

Xi+k−μ=ϕk(Xi−μ)+∑j=1kϕk−jεi+j. X_{i+k}-\mu=\phi^k(X_i-\mu) +\sum_{j=1}^k\phi^{k-j}\varepsilon_{i+j}.

The future innovations are independent of XiX_i. Covary both sides with XiX_i:

Cov(Xi,Xi+k)=ϕkVar(Xi)+∑j=1kϕk−jCov(Xi,εi+j)=ϕkq+0. \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_{i+k}) &=\phi^k\operatorname{Var}(X_i) +\sum_{j=1}^k\phi^{k-j}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,\varepsilon_{i+j})\\ &=\phi^kq+0. \end{aligned}

Autocovariance means covariance of the process with itself at a different time. The stationary lag-kk autocovariance is therefore qϕkq\phi^k for k≥0k\ge0. Correlation divides by the two standard deviations, both q\sqrt q:

ρ(k)=qϕkqq=ϕk. \boxed{\rho(k)=\frac{q\phi^k}{\sqrt q\sqrt q}=\phi^k.}

The coefficient governing the fraction of a deviation retained each tick also governs how correlation decays across ticks. For ϕ=1/2\phi=1/2, lag-one correlation is 1/21/2, lag-two correlation is 1/41/4, and lag-three correlation is 1/81/8.

With a fixed start instead, the same covariance argument yields Cov(Xi,Xi+k)=ϕkVar(Xi)\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_{i+k})=\phi^k\operatorname{Var}(X_i), but the variances at ii and i+ki+k are not generally equal. One cannot automatically divide by qq and declare the correlation to be ϕk\phi^k before stationarity is established.

6.11 What to distinguish when reading an AR(1) formula

For a known current observation, the next-step mean is μ+ϕ(x−μ)\mu+\phi(x-\mu) and the next-step variance is τ2\tau^2. For a fixed start several ticks earlier, accumulated innovation noise gives the larger finite-time variance derived above. Under stationary initialization, the unconditional variance is q=τ2/(1−ϕ2)q=\tau^2/(1-\phi^2).

These are three different conditioning setups. Calling all three quantities “the variance” without saying what is conditioned on makes correct formulas appear contradictory.

Worked check. In the model μ=25\mu=25, ϕ=1/2\phi=1/2, τ2=4\tau^2=4, with fixed X0=29X_0=29, calculate the law of X2X_2. Expanding gives X2=25+(1/2)2(4)+(1/2)ε1+ε2X_2=25+(1/2)^2(4)+(1/2)\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2. Its mean is 2626, and its variance is (1/2)2(4)+4=5(1/2)^2(4)+4=5. Hence X2∼N(26,5)X_2\sim N(26,5). The stationary law would instead be N(25,16/3)N(25,16/3). Knowing X1=27X_1=27 makes the next-step conditional law X2∣X1=27∼N(26,4)X_2\mid X_1=27\sim N(26,4). The same mean 2626 in two of these calculations does not make their variances equal: conditioning on X1X_1 removes uncertainty about the first innovation’s contribution.

Source connection: the AR(1) model and stationarity framework are in MIT Lecture 8. The formulas here are derived from the recursion, including the required squared coefficient in the stationary-variance denominator.

7. Fit the Gaussian AR(1)

IN THIS CHAPTER

  2. 7.2 Write one transition density before writing a product

  4. 7.4 Why the intercept-and-slope form helps
  5. 7.5 Derive the intercept equation
  6. 7.6 Derive the slope equation and prove it minimizes the objective
  7. 7.7 Derive the innovation-variance estimate
  8. 7.8 Convert back to the AR parameters

7.1 The observations are fixed; the model parameters are not

You observe a numerical record x0,x1,…,xnx_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n at equally spaced ticks. Assume the model

Xi=μ+ϕ(Xi−1−μ)+εi,εi∼N(0,τ2), X_i=\mu+\phi(X_{i-1}-\mu)+\varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\tau^2),

with fresh independent Gaussian innovations, independent of the start. Here μ\mu is the mean-reversion level, ϕ\phi is the one-tick retention coefficient, and τ2>0\tau^2>0 is the innovation variance. The Gaussian notation N(m,v)N(m,v) uses variance in its second slot.

Unlike a calculation predicting the next value from known parameters, we now seek the unknown parameter values. The data are the observed states. The candidate parameter vector is (μ,ϕ,τ2)(\mu,\phi,\tau^2). A candidate’s predictions, residuals, and likelihood are quantities computed from that candidate and the fixed data.

We will use a conditional likelihood: the starting value x0x_0 is supplied as a starting condition. There are n+1n+1 recorded values but exactly nn observed transitions. That is why the likelihood below contains nn factors.

The goal is not to make every residual zero. The model allows genuine random noise, and a candidate must account for both its predicted means and its stated uncertainty. Maximum likelihood finds the candidate giving the greatest joint conditional density to the entire record.

7.2 Write one transition density before writing a product

Given the previous observation xi−1x_{i-1}, the candidate mean is

mi=μ+ϕ(xi−1−μ). m_i=\mu+\phi(x_{i-1}-\mu).

All that remains random is the innovation, so the transition density evaluated at the observed next value xix_i is

g(xi∣xi−1;μ,ϕ,τ2)=12πτ2exp[−(xi−mi)22τ2]. g(x_i\mid x_{i-1};\mu,\phi,\tau^2) =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\tau^2}} \exp\left[-\frac{(x_i-m_i)^2}{2\tau^2}\right].

The residual ei=xi−mie_i=x_i-m_i is the observed value minus the candidate’s one-step prediction. The word “candidate” matters: changing μ\mu or ϕ\phi changes every mim_i, hence every residual, even though the observations stay fixed.

The Markov property follows from the recursion and fresh-noise assumption. Applying the probability chain rule and then shortening each conditional history gives

Lc(μ,ϕ,τ2)=∏i=1ng(xi∣xi−1;μ,ϕ,τ2). L_c(\mu,\phi,\tau^2)=\prod_{i=1}^n g(x_i\mid x_{i-1};\mu,\phi,\tau^2).

The states are dependent. This product is valid because it multiplies conditional densities, not because the observations are independent.

7.3 Take the logarithm carefully

For one factor, the logarithm is

loggi=−12log(2πτ2)−ei22τ2. \log g_i=-\frac12\log(2\pi\tau^2)-\frac{e_i^2}{2\tau^2}.

Adding the nn factors’ logarithms gives

ℓ(μ,ϕ,τ2)=−n2log(2πτ2)−12τ2∑i=1n[xi−μ−ϕ(xi−1−μ)]2. \boxed{ \ell(\mu,\phi,\tau^2) =-\frac n2\log(2\pi\tau^2) -\frac{1}{2\tau^2}\sum_{i=1}^n[x_i-\mu-\phi(x_{i-1}-\mu)]^2. }

The same variance appears in every transition because the model assumes a common innovation distribution per tick. With irregular OU gaps, the transition variances will differ, and this particular constant-variance simplification will no longer hold.

If τ2\tau^2 is fixed and positive, the first term does not depend on μ\mu or ϕ\phi. Maximizing the second term is equivalent to minimizing the squared-residual sum, because its coefficient is negative. Thus a Gaussian likelihood creates a least-squares problem. We still need to solve it and then estimate the variance.

7.4 Why the intercept-and-slope form helps

Expand the conditional mean:

mi=μ+ϕxi−1−ϕμ=μ(1−ϕ)+ϕxi−1. \begin{aligned} m_i&=\mu+\phi x_{i-1}-\phi\mu\\ &=\mu(1-\phi)+\phi x_{i-1}. \end{aligned}

Define

a=μ(1−ϕ),b=ϕ. a=\mu(1-\phi),\qquad b=\phi.

Also name the two observed arrays

ui=xi−1,yi=xi,i=1,…,n. u_i=x_{i-1},\qquad y_i=x_i,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.

The uiu_i are the lagged values and the yiy_i are their successors. The same interior observation occurs once as a response and once as a later predictor; that does not make them separate independent samples.

The prediction is now a+buia+bu_i, and the residual sum of squares is

S(a,b)=∑i=1n(yi−a−bui)2. S(a,b)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-a-bu_i)^2.

This is an ordinary intercept-and-slope least-squares objective. The transformation is reversible when b≠1b\ne1:

ϕ=b,μ=a1−b. \phi=b,\qquad \mu=\frac{a}{1-b}.

At ϕ=1\phi=1, the original centered model becomes a random walk with no level parameter; μ\mu disappears. The reverse formula’s division by zero reflects that genuine identification problem.

7.5 Derive the intercept equation

Differentiate SS with respect to aa. For each residual ri=yi−a−buir_i=y_i-a-bu_i, the derivative of ri2r_i^2 is 2ri2r_i times the derivative of rir_i, which is −1-1. Therefore

∂S∂a=−2∑i(yi−a−bui). \frac{\partial S}{\partial a} =-2\sum_i(y_i-a-bu_i).

Set the derivative to zero:

∑iyi−na−b∑iui=0. \sum_i y_i-na-b\sum_i u_i=0.

Define the two means separately,

u‾=1n∑iui,y‾=1n∑iyi. \bar u=\frac1n\sum_i u_i,\qquad \bar y=\frac1n\sum_i y_i.

Divide the equation by nn and solve for aa:

a=y‾−bu‾. \boxed{a=\bar y-b\bar u.}

For any chosen slope, this intercept makes the residuals sum to zero. The fitted line passes through the point (u‾,y‾)(\bar u,\bar y). We have reduced a two-variable minimization to a one-variable problem in bb.

7.6 Derive the slope equation and prove it minimizes the objective

Substitute a=y‾−bu‾a=\bar y-b\bar u into the residual:

yi−a−bui=yi−(y‾−bu‾)−bui=(yi−y‾)−b(ui−u‾). \begin{aligned} y_i-a-bu_i &=y_i-(\bar y-b\bar u)-bu_i\\ &=(y_i-\bar y)-b(u_i-\bar u). \end{aligned}

Introduce three sums, all computed solely from the observed arrays:

Suu=∑i(ui−u‾)2,Suy=∑i(ui−u‾)(yi−y‾), S_{uu}=\sum_i(u_i-\bar u)^2, \qquad S_{uy}=\sum_i(u_i-\bar u)(y_i-\bar y),

Syy=∑i(yi−y‾)2. S_{yy}=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2.

Expanding the squared residuals gives

S(b)=∑i[(yi−y‾)−b(ui−u‾)]2=Syy−2bSuy+b2Suu. \begin{aligned} S(b) &=\sum_i[(y_i-\bar y)-b(u_i-\bar u)]^2\\ &=S_{yy}-2bS_{uy}+b^2S_{uu}. \end{aligned}

Differentiate:

S′(b)=−2Suy+2bSuu. S'(b)=-2S_{uy}+2bS_{uu}.

Provided Suu>0S_{uu}>0, setting this to zero gives

b̂=SuySuu,â=y‾−b̂u‾. \boxed{\hat b=\frac{S_{uy}}{S_{uu}}}, \qquad \boxed{\hat a=\bar y-\hat b\bar u.}

The second derivative is S″(b)=2Suu>0S''(b)=2S_{uu}>0, so this is the unique minimum of the profiled quadratic. Another explicit check is to complete the square:

S(b)=Syy−Suy2Suu+Suu(b−SuySuu)2. S(b)=S_{yy}-\frac{S_{uy}^2}{S_{uu}} +S_{uu}\left(b-\frac{S_{uy}}{S_{uu}}\right)^2.

The last term is nonnegative and becomes zero exactly at the derived slope. This proves global minimization over unrestricted real slopes, rather than merely locating a stationary point.

If Suu=0S_{uu}=0, all lagged observations are equal. Then the data only identify the combination a+buia+bu_i; slope and intercept cannot be separated by this conditional record. The formula’s zero denominator diagnoses a lack of information, not a software inconvenience.

7.7 Derive the innovation-variance estimate

Write v=τ2v=\tau^2 temporarily so there is no ambiguity about whether we differentiate in variance or standard deviation. After choosing â,b̂\hat a,\hat b, let

S*=S(â,b̂). S_*=S(\hat a,\hat b).

The log-likelihood as a function of v>0v>0 is

ℓ(v)=−n2log(2πv)−S*2v. \ell(v)=-\frac n2\log(2\pi v)-\frac{S_*}{2v}.

Differentiate term by term:

ℓ′(v)=−n2v+S*2v2=S*−nv2v2. \ell'(v)=-\frac{n}{2v}+\frac{S_*}{2v^2} =\frac{S_*-nv}{2v^2}.

If S*>0S_*>0, the derivative is positive when v<S*/nv<S_*/n and negative when v>S*/nv>S_*/n. The unique maximum is therefore

τ̂2=S*n. \boxed{\hat\tau^2=\frac{S_*}{n}.}

The denominator is the number of conditional transition factors, nn. A degrees-of-freedom correction answers a different estimation question; it is not what differentiating this likelihood produces.

If S*=0S_*=0, the fit interpolates the record perfectly. The likelihood then increases without bound as vv decreases toward zero, and no positive interior variance MLE exists. A robust implementation should report this degeneracy rather than silently return a valid-looking standard model fit.

Because minimizing SS was the best choice for every fixed v>0v>0, combining the least-squares minimizer with v̂=S*/n\hat v=S_*/n maximizes the joint conditional likelihood whenever the solution is admissible and nondegenerate.

7.8 Convert back to the AR parameters

The conditional estimates are

ϕ̂=b̂,μ̂=â1−b̂,τ̂2=1n∑i(yi−â−b̂ui)2. \boxed{\hat\phi=\hat b,\qquad \hat\mu=\frac{\hat a}{1-\hat b},\qquad \hat\tau^2=\frac1n\sum_i(y_i-\hat a-\hat b u_i)^2.}

The fitted mean-reversion level is not generally the average of all the recorded states. The intercept-and-slope fit is made to paired successive observations, with different lagged and successor means. The transformation μ̂=â/(1−b̂)\hat\mu=\hat a/(1-\hat b) is required by the model’s definition.

When b̂\hat b is close to one, a small change in the fitted intercept or slope can cause a large change in μ̂\hat\mu. The denominator 1−b̂1-\hat b makes this visible. A persistent short record may estimate local movement better than a distant long-run level.

7.9 A complete numerical fit, including every intermediate quantity

Take the record

(x0,x1,x2,x3)=(0,1,1,2). (x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3)=(0,1,1,2).

There are three transitions, so n=3n=3. The lagged array is u=(0,1,1)u=(0,1,1) and the successor array is y=(1,1,2)y=(1,1,2). Their means are u‾=2/3\bar u=2/3 and y‾=4/3\bar y=4/3.

ii uiu_i yiy_i ui−u‾u_i-\bar u yi−y‾y_i-\bar y Product of deviations
1 0 1 −2/3-2/3 −1/3-1/3 2/92/9
2 1 1 1/31/3 −1/3-1/3 −1/9-1/9
3 1 2 1/31/3 2/32/3 2/92/9

Thus

Suy=29−19+29=13,Suu=49+19+19=23. S_{uy}=\frac29-\frac19+\frac29=\frac13, \qquad S_{uu}=\frac49+\frac19+\frac19=\frac23.

The slope is (1/3)/(2/3)=1/2(1/3)/(2/3)=1/2, and the intercept is 4/3−(1/2)(2/3)=14/3-(1/2)(2/3)=1. Convert to the mean-reversion level:

ϕ̂=12,μ̂=11−1/2=2. \hat\phi=\frac12,\qquad \hat\mu=\frac{1}{1-1/2}=2.

The fitted predictions are (1,1.5,1.5)(1,1.5,1.5). Subtract them from the observed successors (1,1,2)(1,1,2) to obtain residuals (0,−0.5,0.5)(0,-0.5,0.5). Their squared sum is 0+0.25+0.25=0.50+0.25+0.25=0.5, hence

τ̂2=0.53=16. \hat\tau^2=\frac{0.5}{3}=\frac16.

The result is the conditional fit (μ̂,ϕ̂,τ̂2)=(2,1/2,1/6)(\hat\mu,\hat\phi,\hat\tau^2)=(2,1/2,1/6). The observed average of all four states is 11, not 22. There is no contradiction: the fitted level is inferred from the relation between each state and its successor, not defined as the unweighted record average.

If we initialized a process at stationarity using these fitted parameters, its state variance would be τ̂2/(1−ϕ̂2)=(1/6)/(3/4)=2/9\hat\tau^2/(1-\hat\phi^2)=(1/6)/(3/4)=2/9. That is a derived model quantity, distinct from the fitted innovation variance 1/61/6.

7.10 Admissibility constraints can change the estimate

The unconstrained regression calculation allows any real slope. A stable causal AR(1) interpretation requires |ϕ|<1|\phi|<1. A fixed-gap mean-reverting scalar OU interpretation requires 0<ϕ<10<\phi<1.

The record (0,2,1,3)(0,2,1,3) gives u‾=1\bar u=1, y‾=2\bar y=2, Suy=−1S_{uy}=-1, and Suu=2S_{uu}=2. Thus its fitted slope is −1/2-1/2. This is an admissible oscillating stable AR(1), but not an exact discretization of the positive mean-reverting scalar OU model. The observed data do not have to produce an admissible OU slope merely because we hoped to use that model.

For a closed allowed slope interval [bmin,bmax][b_{\min},b_{\max}] that excludes the singular value one, the quadratic expression for S(b)S(b) shows how to solve the constrained problem. The optimum is the unrestricted slope projected onto that interval; then the intercept and residual variance must be recomputed at that constrained slope. Changing only ϕ̂\hat\phi while leaving the old μ̂\hat\mu and variance in place generally does not give the constrained likelihood optimum.

If the allowed interval is open, such as (0,1)(0,1), and the best slope would occur at an excluded boundary, the supremum may not be attained. Numerical bounds such as 10−6≤ϕ≤1−10−610^{-6}\le\phi\le1-10^{-6} create a different closed optimization problem. A result at such a bound should be reported as boundary-limited, not as an ordinary interior optimum.

7.11 Conditional and stationary full MLE are not identical calculations

The calculation above conditioned on x0x_0. A stationary Gaussian AR(1) model instead supplies the initial density

X0∼N(μ,τ21−ϕ2),|ϕ|<1. X_0\sim N\left(\mu,\frac{\tau^2}{1-\phi^2}\right),\qquad |\phi|<1.

Its full log-likelihood adds

−12log(2πτ21−ϕ2)−(x0−μ)2(1−ϕ2)2τ2 -\frac12\log\left(\frac{2\pi\tau^2}{1-\phi^2}\right) -\frac{(x_0-\mu)^2(1-\phi^2)}{2\tau^2}

to the conditional log-likelihood. This term depends on all three candidate parameters. It is not a constant merely because x0x_0 is observed. Its presence can change the optimum, so the conditional regression formulas should not be presented as universal formulas for stationary full MLE.

In the short worked record, the conditional fitted level is 22 while the start is 00. A stationary initial-density term would evaluate how plausible that start is under each candidate’s stationary law. Conditional fitting deliberately does not ask that additional question.

7.12 Why an algebraic regression fit does not settle statistical uncertainty

The optimization objective has become a regression sum of squares, but the predictors are lagged values of a dependent process. An innovation εi\varepsilon_i is independent of the previous state used to predict XiX_i, yet it influences XiX_i, which becomes the predictor for the next transition. Thus the full predictor array is not an externally fixed collection independent of every error.

This matters when discussing distributions of estimators, standard errors, and small-sample bias. The algebra above proves what maximizes the conditional Gaussian likelihood. It does not by itself justify every classical fixed-design regression inference formula. Nor does it make ϕ̂\hat\phi unbiased: it is a ratio of random centered sums, and taking the expectation of a ratio is not generally the ratio of expectations.

The fitted slope also is not generally the sample Pearson correlation. If ruyr_{uy} denotes that correlation and su,sys_u,s_y are sample standard deviations calculated with the same divisor, then

b̂=ruysysu. \hat b=r_{uy}\frac{s_y}{s_u}.

The population stationary relation Corr(Xi,Xi+1)=ϕ\operatorname{Corr}(X_i,X_{i+1})=\phi does not force the two finite observed arrays to have equal standard deviations.

The exact lesson is limited but powerful: under the stated conditional Gaussian AR(1) model, estimating the one-step mean reduces to a fully derivable least-squares problem. Irregular observation times will preserve the likelihood principle while changing the form of that regression.

Source connection: MIT Lecture 8 covers likelihood-based time-series estimation. The conditional normal equations, numerical examples, degeneracies, and constrained-slope calculation are derived explicitly above.

8. Refine the clock

IN THIS CHAPTER

  2. 8.2 Derive the drift scaling
  3. 8.3 Derive the noise scaling separately
  4. 8.4 Why the square root is not an arbitrary convention
  5. 8.5 Construct a whole interpolated path
  6. 8.6 Check finite-resolution properties rather than assign limiting ones early
  7. 8.7 What the ordinary central limit theorem establishes
  8. 8.8 Why convergence of paths is a stronger statement

  10. 8.10 Marginal distributions do not determine a process

8.1 Step count is not elapsed time

A random walk Wk=S1+⋯+SkW_k=S_1+\cdots+S_k is indexed by the number of steps. The symbol k=100k=100 means one hundred updates; it says nothing about whether those updates fill one second or one century.

To connect a numerical model to physical time, specify a tick duration δ>0\delta>0. At grid time t=kδt=k\delta, the number of completed ticks is k=t/δk=t/\delta. If the steps have mean mδm_\delta and variance vδv_\delta, independence gives

E[Wk]=kmδ=tδmδ,Var(Wk)=kvδ=tδvδ. E[W_k]=km_\delta=\frac{t}{\delta}m_\delta, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(W_k)=kv_\delta=\frac{t}{\delta}v_\delta.

The subscripts on mδm_\delta and vδv_\delta allow the step distribution to change when we refine the tick size. That change is not a nuisance; it is necessary if different numerical resolutions are meant to approximate the same continuous-time model.

A genuinely discrete model can have a physically meaningful tick duration, such as one transaction or one generation. There is nothing wrong with that. Here the goal is different: we want to make the numerical tick arbitrarily small without changing the intended mean and variance over a fixed physical duration.

8.2 Derive the drift scaling

Suppose the desired deterministic drift rate is aa units of state per unit of time. Over elapsed time tt, the expected accumulated change should be atat.

Our grid model gives expected change (t/δ)mδ(t/\delta)m_\delta. Equating it with atat and canceling tt gives

mδδ=a⇒mδ=aδ. \frac{m_\delta}{\delta}=a \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{m_\delta=a\delta.}

Halving the tick duration doubles the number of ticks within a fixed interval, so the mean change per tick must halve. This is the ordinary rate-times-duration relationship from elementary calculus.

For example, with drift rate a=3a=3 and duration t=2t=2, two ticks of length one each contribute mean three, while two hundred ticks of length 0.010.01 each contribute mean 0.030.03. Both give total expected change six.

8.3 Derive the noise scaling separately

Suppose the desired variance over elapsed time tt is σ2t\sigma^2t, where σ>0\sigma>0 is a noise scale. The grid model gives variance (t/δ)vδ(t/\delta)v_\delta. Equating the two yields

tδvδ=σ2t⇒vδ=σ2δ. \frac{t}{\delta}v_\delta=\sigma^2t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{v_\delta=\sigma^2\delta.}

Variance is proportional to duration. Standard deviation is its square root, so the random step’s standard deviation must be σδ\sigma\sqrt\delta, not σδ\sigma\delta.

To implement both mean and noise scaling, choose i.i.d. variables ξi\xi_i with mean zero and variance one and define a tick’s change by

Si,δ=aδ+σδξi. \boxed{S_{i,\delta}=a\delta+\sigma\sqrt\delta\,\xi_i.}

The first term is deterministic. The second has mean zero and variance σ2δ\sigma^2\delta, since multiplying by σδ\sigma\sqrt\delta multiplies variance by its square. At t=kδt=k\delta, the accumulated process has mean atat and variance σ2t\sigma^2t.

For unit noise scale and one unit of elapsed time:

Tick length δ\delta Number of ticks Step standard deviation δ\sqrt\delta Step variance Total variance
11 11 11 11 11
1/41/4 44 1/21/2 1/41/4 11
1/1001/100 100100 1/101/10 1/1001/100 11

The distribution shapes may still differ at finite resolution, but their intended total variance is calibrated consistently.

8.4 Why the square root is not an arbitrary convention

Suppose instead that random step amplitude were proportional to δα\delta^\alpha, so a centered step were σδαξi\sigma\delta^\alpha\xi_i. Its variance would be σ2δ2α\sigma^2\delta^{2\alpha}. Summing t/δt/\delta independent steps would produce

Var(Wt/δ)=σ2tδ2α−1. \operatorname{Var}(W_{t/\delta}) =\sigma^2t\delta^{2\alpha-1}.

For a finite positive variance limit in this finite-variance diffusion scaling, the exponent must be zero: 2α−1=02\alpha-1=0, hence α=1/2\alpha=1/2.

If α=1\alpha=1, noise is scaled like ordinary drift. Then the total variance is σ2tδ\sigma^2t\delta, which tends to zero: the random fluctuations disappear at fixed times in mean square. If α=0\alpha=0, the step amplitude is not reduced at all, and the total variance grows like 1/δ1/\delta, rather than staying on the intended finite diffusion scale.

This variance calculation selects a regime; it is not a theorem that every possible stochastic scaling limit must be Brownian. Heavy-tailed steps, dependence between steps, or other scaling choices can lead to other limits. Our construction assumes independent finite-variance steps and aims at a continuous Gaussian-noise model.

The dimensions also agree. A drift rate has units “state divided by time,” so aδa\delta has state units. The noise scale has units “state divided by square root of time,” so σδ\sigma\sqrt\delta also has state units. Adding the two is dimensionally consistent.

8.5 Construct a whole interpolated path

Take independent fair steps ξi∈{−1,1}\xi_i\in\{-1,1\} and let Wk=∑i=1kξiW_k=\sum_{i=1}^k\xi_i. Choose resolution nn ticks per unit time, so δ=1/n\delta=1/n. Define a process on the grid by

Zn(k/n)=Wkn. Z_n(k/n)=\frac{W_k}{\sqrt n}.

Equivalently, each tick has an effective step ξi/n\xi_i/\sqrt n of variance 1/n1/n. The normalization can be placed in each step or outside the accumulated sum; those constructions are identical.

To obtain a value between grid times, join successive grid positions by a straight line. If t=(k+r)/nt=(k+r)/n for 0≤r<10\le r<1, the linear interpolation is

Zn(t)=Wk+rξk+1n. \boxed{Z_n(t)=\frac{W_k+r\xi_{k+1}}{\sqrt n}.}

At r=0r=0 this gives the left endpoint Wk/nW_k/\sqrt n. At r=1r=1 it gives the right endpoint Wk+1/nW_{k+1}/\sqrt n. The interpolated sample path is continuous for each finite nn, but it is piecewise linear and not yet a Brownian path.

8.6 Check finite-resolution properties rather than assign limiting ones early

At a grid point t=k/nt=k/n, the variance is k/n=tk/n=t. Between grid points, independence of WkW_k and ξk+1\xi_{k+1} gives

Var(Zn(t))=Var(Wk)+r2Var(ξk+1)n=k+r2n. \operatorname{Var}(Z_n(t)) =\frac{\operatorname{Var}(W_k)+r^2\operatorname{Var}(\xi_{k+1})}{n} =\frac{k+r^2}{n}.

The target variance tt equals (k+r)/n(k+r)/n, not (k+r2)/n(k+r^2)/n. Their difference is

t−Var(Zn(t))=r−r2n, t-\operatorname{Var}(Z_n(t))=\frac{r-r^2}{n},

which is at most 1/(4n)1/(4n) because r−r2=r(1−r)r-r^2=r(1-r) has maximum 1/41/4. Thus the discrepancy vanishes with refinement, but it is not zero at every finite resolution.

For n=4n=4 and t=1/8t=1/8, we have k=0k=0 and r=1/2r=1/2. The interpolated variance is (1/4)/4=1/16(1/4)/4=1/16, while t=1/8t=1/8. This concrete discrepancy prevents us from claiming that the interpolated walk already has exact Brownian variance at all times.

Likewise, two disjoint subintervals lying inside one grid cell share the same random slope ξk+1n\xi_{k+1}\sqrt n. Their increments are not independent. Increments over disjoint grid-aligned blocks are independent because they use disjoint steps. The distinction between grid points and interpolated points must be respected before taking a limit.

8.7 What the ordinary central limit theorem establishes

The central limit theorem for i.i.d. zero-mean unit-variance steps states

Wkk→dN(0,1). \frac{W_k}{\sqrt k}\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1).

At time one, Zn(1)=Wn/nZ_n(1)=W_n/\sqrt n, so the theorem directly gives convergence to N(0,1)N(0,1).

For fixed t>0t>0, let k=⌊nt⌋k=\lfloor nt\rfloor, the greatest integer not exceeding ntnt. Then

Wkn=Wkkkn. \frac{W_k}{\sqrt n} =\frac{W_k}{\sqrt k}\sqrt{\frac kn}.

The first factor approaches a standard normal distribution; the deterministic second factor approaches t\sqrt t. The resulting distribution approaches N(0,t)N(0,t). The interpolation contribution has magnitude at most 1/n1/\sqrt n for our ±1\pm1 steps, so it disappears as nn grows. Thus the interpolated Zn(t)Z_n(t) has the same fixed-time limit.

This establishes a one-time distributional limit. It does not mean a particular walk outcome becomes a Gaussian number, nor does it by itself prove convergence of the entire path. A probability distribution is a description across repeated outcomes, not a shape drawn by one trajectory.

8.8 Why convergence of paths is a stronger statement

To describe a process, we need joint behavior at different times. For ordered times t1<t2<⋯<tmt_1<t_2<\cdots<t_m, disjoint increments of the scaled walk come from separate blocks of independent steps. Their variances approach the interval lengths. This suggests jointly independent Gaussian increments in the limit, and therefore the desired joint distributions of positions obtained by adding those increments.

Even matching all finite collections of times is not, on its own, a complete proof about continuous functions under a path topology. One must also control the paths’ oscillations so that probability does not concentrate on increasingly irregular behavior invisible to a finite observation set.

The functional central limit theorem, also called Donsker’s theorem, supplies the stronger result: on a fixed bounded time interval, these normalized, linearly interpolated i.i.d. finite-variance walks converge in distribution as random continuous functions to Brownian motion. The usual topology measures the maximum difference between functions over the whole interval.

This theorem is stated here, not proved in its full functional-analytic generality. What we have derived is the normalization, the finite-time limits, and the reason a further path-level theorem is required. None of the later OU calculations will pretend that a one-variable CLT proved an entire process construction.

8.9 Understand a process as a random function

For one experiment outcome ω\omega, a stochastic process assigns a trajectory t↦Xt(ω)t\mapsto X_t(\omega). There are three distinct operations.

If you fix the time tt and let the experiment vary, XtX_t is a random variable. If you fix the outcome ω\omega and vary time, Xt(ω)X_t(\omega) is an ordinary function of tt. If you fix both, Xt(ω)X_t(\omega) is one number.

For a three-step fair walk, the outcome could be the step sequence (1,−1,1)(1,-1,1). Its path is the function on times 0,1,2,30,1,2,3 taking values 0,1,0,10,1,0,1. The outcome is not the same object as its value at time three, which is just the number one. The random variable W3W_3 is the rule that reads the final value from whichever outcome is realized.

One can choose the sample space to be a space of paths itself. Then an event is a set of paths, such as “paths ending above zero” or “paths that stay nonnegative throughout the interval.” Assigning probabilities to such sets is the path-space viewpoint.

8.10 Marginal distributions do not determine a process

A marginal distribution describes the state at one time without describing its relationship to states at other times. Two continuous processes can have the same marginal distribution at every time and still have very different dependence.

Let Z,Z1,Z2Z,Z_1,Z_2 be independent standard normal variables. Define

Ut=Z,Vt=Z1cost+Z2sint. U_t=Z, \qquad V_t=Z_1\cos t+Z_2\sin t.

For every fixed tt, Ut∼N(0,1)U_t\sim N(0,1). The variable VtV_t is a linear combination of independent Gaussians, so it is Gaussian with mean zero and variance cos2t+sin2t=1\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1. Thus Vt∼N(0,1)V_t\sim N(0,1) too.

But UtU_t is a constant path: once its value is drawn, it never changes. The second process generally varies with time. Their covariances expose the difference:

Cov(Us,Ut)=1, \operatorname{Cov}(U_s,U_t)=1,

whereas

Cov(Vs,Vt)=cosscost+sinssint=cos(t−s). \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(V_s,V_t) &=\cos s\cos t+\sin s\sin t\\ &=\cos(t-s). \end{aligned}

Therefore giving a distribution such as Xt∼N(0,t)X_t\sim N(0,t) for every tt would not, by itself, specify Brownian motion. We also need the joint relationship between increments and path continuity.

8.11 Numerical ticks and observation gaps are not interchangeable

The symbol δ\delta in this chapter is a numerical resolution used to build an approximation. Later, Δi=ti−ti−1\Delta_i=t_i-t_{i-1} will denote an actual gap between recorded observations. A fine simulation grid and a sparse observation grid serve different purposes.

For a model with an exact transition distribution, such as OU, one can simulate directly between the required observation times. There is no need to insert a tiny Euler grid merely to obtain correct endpoint observations. The continuum model describes the process between recordings; its transition law already summarizes the effect of the unobserved interval.

Worked check. You want drift rate a=2a=2, noise scale σ=3\sigma=3, and total time T=1T=1. With tick size δ=1/100\delta=1/100, each step should be 0.02+0.3ξi0.02+0.3\xi_i, where E[ξi]=0E[\xi_i]=0 and Var(ξi)=1\operatorname{Var}(\xi_i)=1. One hundred independent steps have mean 22 and variance 100(0.32)=9100(0.3^2)=9. Using 0.03ξi0.03\xi_i instead would give variance 0.090.09, one hundred times too small. That error comes from scaling noise by δ\delta instead of δ\sqrt\delta.

Source connection: the path-space viewpoint and Brownian scaling construction are discussed in MIT Lecture 17, sections 1–2. The normalization and finite-interpolation corrections are calculated explicitly here. The functional limit theorem is identified as an additional theorem rather than silently inferred from a scalar CLT.

9. Read Brownian motion correctly

IN THIS CHAPTER

  1. 9.1 Define the process before using its notation
  2. 9.2 The distribution at one time
  3. 9.3 Independent increments do not mean independent positions
  4. 9.4 Joint Gaussianity: why means and covariances become enough
  5. 9.5 Derive the conditional transition law and the Markov property
  6. 9.6 Covariance of arbitrary increments is overlap length
  7. 9.7 Why Brownian motion is not stationary
  8. 9.8 Why there is no ordinary Brownian velocity

  10. 9.10 The meaning of the informal symbol (dB)2=dt(dB)^2=dt

9.1 Define the process before using its notation

Brownian motion is a mathematical model for continuously accumulated random fluctuations. The word “continuous” refers to its sample paths, not to smoothness or differentiability. We define the process through its probability properties rather than by pretending there is a smallest next instant of time.

A standard Brownian motion (Bt)t≥0(B_t)_{t\ge0} has the following properties. It starts at B0=0B_0=0. Its paths are continuous with probability one. Its increments over disjoint time intervals are mutually independent. Finally, for every 0≤s<t0\le s<t,

Bt−Bs∼N(0,t−s). \boxed{B_t-B_s\sim N(0,t-s).}

The notation N(m,v)N(m,v) means Gaussian with mean mm and variance vv. Thus the increment’s standard deviation is t−s\sqrt{t-s}. The increment distribution depends only on elapsed time, not on when the interval starts. This is stationary increments.

“Standard” fixes the variance rate to one. Multiplying by a constant σ\sigma gives increments of variance σ2(t−s)\sigma^2(t-s). Adding a deterministic drift atat changes the increment mean to a(t−s)a(t-s).

Existence of a process satisfying the definition is a theorem. The normalized random-walk construction motivates it and, with a functional limit theorem, provides one route to it. The defining properties will be the starting assumptions for the derivations in this chapter.

9.2 The distribution at one time

Because B0=0B_0=0, the state at time tt is itself the increment over [0,t][0,t]:

Bt=Bt−B0∼N(0,t). B_t=B_t-B_0\sim N(0,t).

Therefore

E[Bt]=0,Var(Bt)=t,E[Bt2]=t. E[B_t]=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(B_t)=t, \qquad E[B_t^2]=t.

The last equality follows from Var(U)=E[U2]−(E[U])2\operatorname{Var}(U)=E[U^2]-(E[U])^2 and the zero mean. It is not a new independent assumption.

At time four, the distribution is N(0,4)N(0,4) and its standard deviation is two. To calculate a probability, standardize:

P(B4>2)=P(B42>1)=P(Z>1),Z∼N(0,1). P(B_4>2)=P\left(\frac{B_4}{2}>1\right)=P(Z>1), \qquad Z\sim N(0,1).

If Φ(z)=P(Z≤z)\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z) denotes the standard normal distribution function, this is 1−Φ(1)1-\Phi(1), approximately 0.1590.159. The process mean staying zero does not imply that a realized path stays close to zero; its one-time standard deviation grows as t\sqrt t.

An interval such as [−1.96t,1.96t][-1.96\sqrt t,1.96\sqrt t] contains approximately 95%95\% of the distribution at a specified single time tt. It is not automatically a band with 95%95\% probability of containing the entire path over many times. A pathwise event places multiple simultaneous restrictions and is a different probability question.

9.3 Independent increments do not mean independent positions

Take 0<s<t0<s<t and split the later position into two pieces:

Bt=Bs+(Bt−Bs). B_t=B_s+(B_t-B_s).

The first piece is the increment over [0,s][0,s]; the second is the increment over [s,t][s,t]. These pieces are independent. Nevertheless, BsB_s and BtB_t are not independent because the second position includes the first piece.

Covariance quantifies the shared contribution. By its centered definition, covariance is linear in either argument and Cov(U,U)=Var(U)\operatorname{Cov}(U,U)=\operatorname{Var}(U). Therefore

Cov(Bs,Bt)=Cov(Bs,Bs+(Bt−Bs))=Var(Bs)+Cov(Bs,Bt−Bs)=s+0=s. \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(B_s,B_t) &=\operatorname{Cov}(B_s,B_s+(B_t-B_s))\\ &=\operatorname{Var}(B_s)+\operatorname{Cov}(B_s,B_t-B_s)\\ &=s+0\\ &=s. \end{aligned}

The zero cross term uses independence of the increments. Reversing the roles of ss and tt when necessary gives

Cov(Bs,Bt)=min(s,t). \boxed{\operatorname{Cov}(B_s,B_t)=\min(s,t).}

For positive s≤ts\le t, the correlation is

Corr(Bs,Bt)=sst=st. \operatorname{Corr}(B_s,B_t) =\frac{s}{\sqrt s\sqrt t}=\sqrt{\frac st}.

At s=0s=0, the initial value has variance zero, so a correlation coefficient involving B0B_0 is undefined; the covariance formula still gives zero. The distinction between covariance and correlation includes their denominators and domains, not just their names.

9.4 Joint Gaussianity: why means and covariances become enough

Choose times 0=t0<t1<⋯<tm0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m. Define increments Uj=Btj−Btj−1U_j=B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}}. By the Brownian definition, these are independent centered Gaussian variables with variances tj−tj−1t_j-t_{j-1}. The positions are their partial sums:

Bt1=U1,Bt2=U1+U2,…,Btm=U1+⋯+Um. B_{t_1}=U_1,\quad B_{t_2}=U_1+U_2,\quad\ldots,\quad B_{t_m}=U_1+\cdots+U_m.

Any linear combination of the positions is therefore a linear combination of independent Gaussian increments, and is Gaussian. This is the defining property of a jointly Gaussian vector. For such vectors, the mean vector and covariance matrix determine the distribution.

For example,

(B1B3B4)has mean (000)and covariance (111133134). \begin{pmatrix}B_1\\B_3\\B_4\end{pmatrix} \quad\text{has mean }\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix} \quad\text{and covariance } \begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\1&3&3\\1&3&4\end{pmatrix}.

The off-diagonal entries are the lengths of shared history. The diagonal entries are the variances at their respective times.

The qualification “jointly Gaussian” cannot be dropped. Knowing that each separate state is Gaussian does not by itself imply that every linear combination is Gaussian or that covariances determine all dependence. Here joint Gaussianity was derived from the independent Gaussian increments.

9.5 Derive the conditional transition law and the Markov property

Suppose the value at time ss is known to be bb. The decomposition Bt=Bs+(Bt−Bs)B_t=B_s+(B_t-B_s) becomes a fixed starting value plus a fresh Gaussian increment:

Bt∣Bs=b∼N(b,t−s). \boxed{B_t\mid B_s=b\sim N(b,t-s).}

For example, before any observation, B5∼N(0,5)B_5\sim N(0,5). After observing B2=3B_2=3, the remaining uncertainty is the increment over three time units, so B5∣B2=3∼N(3,3)B_5\mid B_2=3\sim N(3,3). Conditioning changes both the mean and the variance.

More generally, the future increments are independent of the information generated by all Brownian values up to time ss. That accumulated information is often written ℱs\mathcal F_s and called the Brownian filtration at ss. A filtration is an increasing family of information sets: more time reveals more observations.

Once BsB_s is supplied, the older Brownian history cannot improve the distributional prediction of BtB_t. This establishes the Markov property. It is a consequence of the increment construction, not a separate appeal to independence of the positions.

9.6 Covariance of arbitrary increments is overlap length

Let U=Bb−BaU=B_b-B_a and V=Bd−BcV=B_d-B_c, with a<ba<b and c<dc<d. Expand covariance using the position covariance already derived:

Cov(U,V)=Cov(Bb,Bd)−Cov(Bb,Bc)−Cov(Ba,Bd)+Cov(Ba,Bc)=min(b,d)−min(b,c)−min(a,d)+min(a,c). \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(U,V) &=\operatorname{Cov}(B_b,B_d)-\operatorname{Cov}(B_b,B_c)\\ &\quad-\operatorname{Cov}(B_a,B_d)+\operatorname{Cov}(B_a,B_c)\\ &=\min(b,d)-\min(b,c)-\min(a,d)+\min(a,c). \end{aligned}

This expression equals the length of the overlap of the intervals [a,b][a,b] and [c,d][c,d]. If the intervals are disjoint apart from an endpoint, the covariance is zero, and Brownian independent increments give independence. For overlapping intervals, the common Brownian fluctuation contributes to both changes.

For U=B3−B1U=B_3-B_1 and V=B4−B2V=B_4-B_2, the overlap is [2,3][2,3], of length one. Substitution confirms it:

Cov(U,V)=3−2−1+1=1. \operatorname{Cov}(U,V)=3-2-1+1=1.

Each increment has variance two, so their correlation is 1/21/2. This example distinguishes “an increment” from “an independent increment relative to another specified interval.”

9.7 Why Brownian motion is not stationary

A stationary process has joint distributions unchanged when all time arguments are shifted together. In particular, its one-time distribution cannot depend on absolute time. Brownian motion fails that condition because Var(Bt)=t\operatorname{Var}(B_t)=t.

Its increments are stationary because Bs+h−Bs∼N(0,h)B_{s+h}-B_s\sim N(0,h) for every starting time ss. The quantity being shifted in this statement is an interval change, not an absolute position. These two notions of stationarity concern different objects.

A related but different symmetry is Brownian scaling. For a positive constant cc, define B̃t=Bct/c\widetilde B_t=B_{ct}/\sqrt c. Its increments satisfy

B̃t−B̃s=Bct−Bcsc∼N(0,c(t−s)c)=N(0,t−s). \widetilde B_t-\widetilde B_s =\frac{B_{ct}-B_{cs}}{\sqrt c} \sim N\left(0,\frac{c(t-s)}c\right)=N(0,t-s).

They remain independent over disjoint intervals, the paths remain continuous, and the start remains zero. Hence B̃\widetilde B is also standard Brownian motion. This is equality of process laws, not an assertion that Bct/cB_{ct}/\sqrt c and BtB_t are equal on each particular path.

9.8 Why there is no ordinary Brownian velocity

For an ordinary differentiable function x(t)x(t), the difference quotient [x(t+h)−x(t)]/h[x(t+h)-x(t)]/h approaches a finite derivative as h→0h\to0. Brownian increments behave differently.

For a fixed deterministic time tt and h>0h>0, define

Qh=Bt+h−Bth. Q_h=\frac{B_{t+h}-B_t}{h}.

The numerator is N(0,h)N(0,h). Dividing by hh multiplies variance by 1/h21/h^2, giving

Qh∼N(0,1/h). \boxed{Q_h\sim N(0,1/h).}

Its typical magnitude is 1/h1/\sqrt h, rather than a finite slope. But variance divergence alone is not a general proof that random variables cannot converge. We can make a more precise argument using the actual Gaussian law.

For any fixed finite M>0M>0,

P(|Qh|≤M)=P(|Z|≤Mh),Z∼N(0,1). P(|Q_h|\le M)=P(|Z|\le M\sqrt h),\qquad Z\sim N(0,1).

The standard normal density is at most 1/2π1/\sqrt{2\pi}. The interval [−Mh,Mh][-M\sqrt h,M\sqrt h] has length 2Mh2M\sqrt h, so

P(|Qh|≤M)≤2Mh2π→0. P(|Q_h|\le M)\le\frac{2M\sqrt h}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\to0.

If a finite derivative existed at this fixed tt, then along the sequence h=1/nh=1/n the quotients would eventually be bounded by some integer MM. For fixed integers M,KM,K, the event that |Q1/n|≤M|Q_{1/n}|\le M for every n≥Kn\ge K is contained in each individual event |Q1/n|≤M|Q_{1/n}|\le M. Its probability is therefore no larger than arbitrarily small such probabilities, and hence is zero. Taking the countable union over MM and KK shows that a finite derivative at this fixed time has probability zero.

The stronger theorem is that a Brownian path is almost surely nowhere differentiable: with probability one there is no time with a finite ordinary derivative. The fixed-time calculation alone does not prove that stronger statement, because an uncountable union of probability-zero events need not have probability zero. The stronger theorem is a genuine additional regularity result. We will use the fact, not pretend that the fixed-time argument proved more than it did.

9.9 Squared increments do not disappear

A second calculation explains why ordinary differential manipulations can fail. Partition [0,T][0,T] into deterministic intervals with endpoints 0=t0<t1<⋯<tm=T0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T. Let hj=tj+1−tjh_j=t_{j+1}-t_j and ΔBj=Btj+1−Btj\Delta B_j=B_{t_{j+1}}-B_{t_j}. Consider

Q=∑j=0m−1(ΔBj)2. Q=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}(\Delta B_j)^2.

Each increment is N(0,hj)N(0,h_j), so E[(ΔBj)2]=hjE[(\Delta B_j)^2]=h_j. Therefore

E[Q]=∑jhj=T. E[Q]=\sum_j h_j=T.

To see whether QQ concentrates near TT, calculate its variance. If Z∼N(0,1)Z\sim N(0,1), then E[Z4]=3E[Z^4]=3. This follows by integration by parts: writing the standard normal density as φ\varphi with φ′(z)=−zφ(z)\varphi'(z)=-z\varphi(z),

∫z4φ(z)dz=−∫z3φ′(z)dz=3∫z2φ(z)dz=3, \int z^4\varphi(z)\,dz =-\int z^3\varphi'(z)\,dz =3\int z^2\varphi(z)\,dz=3,

where the integrals run over the real line and the Gaussian tails make the boundary term vanish. Thus E[(ΔBj)4]=3hj2E[(\Delta B_j)^4]=3h_j^2, and

Var((ΔBj)2)=3hj2−hj2=2hj2. \operatorname{Var}((\Delta B_j)^2)=3h_j^2-h_j^2=2h_j^2.

The squared increments are independent because the underlying increments are independent. Hence

Var(Q)=2∑jhj2≤2(maxjhj)∑jhj=2Tmaxjhj. \operatorname{Var}(Q)=2\sum_jh_j^2 \le2\left(\max_jh_j\right)\sum_jh_j =2T\max_jh_j.

As the largest interval length tends to zero,

E[(Q−T)2]→0. \boxed{E[(Q-T)^2]\to0.}

This is convergence in mean square: the expected squared error tends to zero. In particular it implies convergence in probability, because P(|Q−T|>ϵ)≤E[(Q−T)2]/ϵ2P(|Q-T|>\epsilon)\le E[(Q-T)^2]/\epsilon^2. The limiting value TT is Brownian motion’s quadratic variation along these refining deterministic partitions.

For a smooth function with bounded derivative |x′|≤C|x'|\le C on [0,T][0,T], each increment satisfies |Δxj|≤Chj|\Delta x_j|\le Ch_j. Thus ∑j(Δxj)2≤C2∑jhj2→0\sum_j(\Delta x_j)^2\le C^2\sum_jh_j^2\to0. Brownian motion instead leaves a nonzero accumulated squared-increment term. This difference is the source of the extra second-order terms in Itô calculus.

9.10 The meaning of the informal symbol (dB)2=dt(dB)^2=dt

The expression (dBt)2=dt(dB_t)^2=dt is often used as a mnemonic for quadratic variation. It is not a pathwise equality saying the square of each small Brownian increment equals its interval length. A single increment is random, and its square fluctuates.

The rigorous calculation above says that the sum of squared increments over a refining partition approaches total elapsed time in a specified mode of convergence. That is the fact a valid stochastic-calculus argument must ultimately use. We will not treat dBdB as an ordinary infinitesimal whose algebra is self-explanatory.

9.11 Exact simulation at a finite set of times

For deterministic times 0=t0<t1<⋯<tn0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n, draw independent standard normal variables Z1,…,ZnZ_1,\ldots,Z_n and set

Bti=Bti−1+ti−ti−1Zi. B_{t_i}=B_{t_{i-1}}+\sqrt{t_i-t_{i-1}}\,Z_i.

Each increment has the required Gaussian law and is independent of the others. Thus the resulting finite vector has the exact Brownian distribution at those times. A line drawn between the simulated points is only a visual interpolation; it does not recreate the unobserved Brownian path inside each interval.

Worked check. Compute Cov(B2,B5)\operatorname{Cov}(B_2,B_5) and the law of B5B_5 after observing B2=−1B_2=-1. The covariance is the shared time length two. The future increment is independent N(0,3)N(0,3), so the conditional law is N(−1,3)N(-1,3). The unconditional law is N(0,5)N(0,5). Now compare increments B2−B0B_2-B_0 and B5−B2B_5-B_2: they are independent, even though the positions B2B_2 and B5B_5 are not. Every answer follows from identifying what randomness is shared and what randomness is new.

Source connection: Brownian motion and its regularity are discussed in MIT Lecture 17; quadratic variation motivates Lecture 18. Covariance, conditional prediction, the fixed-time derivative argument, and the mean-square quadratic-variation calculation are derived above.

IN THIS CHAPTER
