10.1 There are two different unknowns in this project

A stochastic differential equation, or SDE, specifies how a random process evolves. For example,

dXt=θ(μ−Xt)dt+σdBt dX_t=\theta(\mu-X_t)\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t

is the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model. The state XtX_t is a random quantity at time tt. The parameters θ>0\theta>0, μ∈ℝ\mu\in\mathbb R, and σ>0\sigma>0 control the model. The process BtB_t is standard Brownian motion: it starts at zero, has continuous paths, and has independent Gaussian increments of variance equal to elapsed time.

Solving the SDE means expressing the process XX in terms of a given starting value, given parameters, and the driving Brownian noise. Estimating the parameters means using observations of XX to infer the unknown values of θ,μ,σ\theta,\mu,\sigma. These tasks are connected, but they are not the same operation. We usually solve or characterize the model first so that we can later calculate its likelihood.

Before doing either task, we need to give the displayed differential equation a precise meaning. In particular, dBtdB_t cannot be treated as an ordinary derivative times dtdt, because Brownian paths do not possess an ordinary finite derivative.

10.2 Start with the meaning of an ordinary differential equation

Consider the ordinary equation

x′(t)=g(t),x(0)=x0, x'(t)=g(t),\qquad x(0)=x_0,

with continuous gg. Its integral form, by the fundamental theorem of calculus, is

x(t)=x0+∫0tg(s)ds. x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t g(s)\,ds.

The integral accumulates changes over time. On a partition 0=t0<⋯<tm=t0=t_0<\cdots<t_m=t, the sum

∑j=0m−1g(tj)(tj+1−tj) \sum_{j=0}^{m-1}g(t_j)(t_{j+1}-t_j)

approximates the accumulated change. Each summand is a rate multiplied by a duration. As the largest interval length tends to zero, the sum tends to the ordinary integral.

The shorthand dx=g(t)dtdx=g(t)dt is compatible with this accumulation interpretation. It is not a license to regard dxdx and dtdt as arbitrary independent algebraic symbols. The underlying derivative or integral statement determines what operations are valid.

For example, dx=3dtdx=3dt with x(0)=1x(0)=1 means x(t)=1+3tx(t)=1+3t. The equation dx=2tdtdx=2t\,dt means x(t)=x0+t2x(t)=x_0+t^2. Both are solved by integrating known functions of time.

10.3 A random path can still have an ordinary time integral

Suppose XsX_s is a continuous random process. For one realized outcome ω\omega, the function s↦Xs(ω)s\mapsto X_s(\omega) is a continuous ordinary function. Therefore

∫0tXs(ω)ds \int_0^t X_s(\omega)\,ds

exists as an ordinary time integral on a bounded interval. The result is random across different outcomes, but the integration variable is still ordinary time.

Thus the OU drift integral

θ∫0t(μ−Xs)ds \theta\int_0^t(\mu-X_s)\,ds

does not require differentiating XX. A continuous path can be integrated even when it cannot be differentiated. This distinction is important: roughness of the path does not make every integral involving it mysterious.

The new issue is an integral against Brownian increments, written ∫bsdBs\int b_s\,dB_s. Its increments come from the random integrator BB, rather than from time intervals dsds. We will define that object explicitly in Chapter 11, beginning with constant and step-function weights.

10.4 Constant Brownian weight: the sum telescopes exactly

For any partition of [0,t][0,t],

∑j=0m−1(Btj+1−Btj)=(Bt1−B0)+(Bt2−Bt1)+⋯+(Bt−Btm−1)=Bt−B0=Bt. \begin{aligned} \sum_{j=0}^{m-1}(B_{t_{j+1}}-B_{t_j}) &=(B_{t_1}-B_0)+(B_{t_2}-B_{t_1})+\cdots+(B_t-B_{t_{m-1}})\\ &=B_t-B_0\\ &=B_t. \end{aligned}

Every interior Brownian value appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign. The cancellation is exact at every partition; no derivative is involved.

Multiplying by a constant σ\sigma gives

∫0tσdBs=σ(Bt−B0)=σBt. \int_0^t\sigma\,dB_s=\sigma(B_t-B_0)=\sigma B_t.

For this constant integrand, the stochastic integral is already completely understandable as an accumulated increment sum. We do not need a general Itô integral construction merely to read this case.

Contrast this with ∫0tσBsds\int_0^t\sigma B_s\,ds. That is an ordinary time integral of the Brownian path and is not generally equal to σBt\sigma B_t. The placement of BsB_s and the differential matters: weighting elapsed time by a Brownian value is different from accumulating Brownian increments.

10.5 The precise meaning of additive-noise SDEs

For a constant noise scale σ\sigma, the equation

dXt=a(Xt,t)dt+σdBt,X0=x0, dX_t=a(X_t,t)\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t,\qquad X_0=x_0,

means

Xt=x0+∫0ta(Xs,s)ds+σBt. \boxed{X_t=x_0+\int_0^t a(X_s,s)\,ds+\sigma B_t.}

A solution is a process that satisfies this integral equation, with a continuous version and the specified initial value. Its value at time tt uses the initial condition and noise up to time tt, not future Brownian increments.

A process that uses only information available up to its current time is called adapted to that information flow. Formally, the information available at time tt is represented by a filtration ℱt\mathcal F_t, an increasing family of collections of events. For our linear model, one can think of ℱt\mathcal F_t as information from X0X_0 and all Brownian values observed by time tt. No advanced filtration calculation is needed to understand the examples here.

The integral equation is the definition behind the differential shorthand. We should not divide the displayed SDE by dtdt and interpret dBt/dtdB_t/dt as a finite ordinary velocity. Over a short interval of length hh, the Brownian increment has standard deviation h\sqrt h. Dividing by hh produces standard deviation 1/h1/\sqrt h, not a finite derivative.

10.6 Solve constant drift plus constant noise

Consider

dXt=adt+σdBt,X0=x0, dX_t=a\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t,\qquad X_0=x_0,

where aa and σ\sigma are fixed constants. Its integral form is

Xt=x0+∫0tads+σBt=x0+at+σBt. X_t=x_0+\int_0^t a\,ds+\sigma B_t=x_0+at+\sigma B_t.

The right side now contains only known constants and the given Brownian process. That is an explicit solution.

Because Bt∼N(0,t)B_t\sim N(0,t), scaling and shifting give

Xt∼N(x0+at,σ2t). \boxed{X_t\sim N(x_0+at,\sigma^2t).}

For a later time s+hs+h, subtract the solution at ss:

Xs+h−Xs=ah+σ(Bs+h−Bs). X_{s+h}-X_s=ah+\sigma(B_{s+h}-B_s).

The future Brownian increment is independent of the past, so

Xs+h∣Xs=x∼N(x+ah,σ2h). X_{s+h}\mid X_s=x\sim N(x+ah,\sigma^2h).

Take x0=1x_0=1, a=3a=3, and σ=2\sigma=2. Then Xt=1+3t+2BtX_t=1+3t+2B_t and Xt∼N(1+3t,4t)X_t\sim N(1+3t,4t). At t=2t=2, the mean is seven and the variance is eight. The noise standard deviation is 222\sqrt2, not eight and not four.

If the drift is a deterministic time function instead, such as a(s)=2sa(s)=2s, the same reading gives Xt=x0+t2+σBtX_t=x_0+t^2+\sigma B_t. Its mean is x0+t2x_0+t^2 and its variance remains σ2t\sigma^2t. Randomness does not interfere with the ordinary integration of a known drift function.

10.7 Read the OU equation term by term

For OU, the drift is a(x,t)=θ(μ−x)a(x,t)=\theta(\mu-x) and the noise scale is constant. Its integral equation is

Xt=X0+θ∫0t(μ−Xs)ds+σBt. \boxed{X_t=X_0+\theta\int_0^t(\mu-X_s)\,ds+\sigma B_t.}

The starting value contributes X0X_0. At each time ss, the discrepancy from the target is μ−Xs\mu-X_s. The parameter θ\theta converts that discrepancy into a rate of expected correction. Integrating the rate over time accumulates the drift contribution. The last term accumulates the independent Brownian disturbances.

If the state is above μ\mu, the drift coefficient is negative; if below μ\mu, it is positive. But the noise can move the state in either direction, so this does not require every observed increment to point toward the target.

The equation is not yet an explicit solution because XsX_s appears inside the integral on the right. It is a self-consistent relationship that the whole process must satisfy. Merely giving it an integral meaning does not remove that unknown. Chapter 12 will solve this dependence using an ordinary integrating-factor argument after separating the additive Brownian term.

10.8 Exact increments and frozen-drift approximations are different

Subtract the OU integral equation at time tt from the equation at time t+ht+h:

Xt+h−Xt=θ∫tt+h(μ−Xs)ds+σ(Bt+h−Bt). \boxed{ X_{t+h}-X_t =\theta\int_t^{t+h}(\mu-X_s)\,ds +\sigma(B_{t+h}-B_t). }

This is an exact equality. The drift depends on the path throughout the interval, not only on its starting value.

A simple approximation replaces the evolving XsX_s inside the drift integral by the starting state XtX_t:

Xt+h−Xt≈θ(μ−Xt)h+σ(Bt+h−Bt). X_{t+h}-X_t \approx\theta(\mu-X_t)h+\sigma(B_{t+h}-B_t).

The approximation is called an Euler–Maruyama step. The exact difference between the true drift integral and its frozen version is

θ∫tt+h(Xt−Xs)ds. \theta\int_t^{t+h}(X_t-X_s)\,ds.

This is generally nonzero at a finite hh. Under continuity it becomes small relative to hh along a fixed path as h→0h\to0, because

|θ∫tt+h(Xt−Xs)ds|≤θhsupt≤s≤t+h|Xt−Xs|. \left|\theta\int_t^{t+h}(X_t-X_s)ds\right| \le\theta h\sup_{t\le s\le t+h}|X_t-X_s|.

The supremum tends to zero by continuity. This local observation explains the approximation; establishing global error rates for a numerical scheme is a further question.

An Euler approximation process on grid times can be defined exactly by

Xi+1E=XiE+θ(μ−XiE)hi+σhiZi, X^{E}_{i+1}=X^{E}_i+\theta(\mu-X^{E}_i)h_i+\sigma\sqrt{h_i}\,Z_i,

where ZiZ_i are independent standard normals. The equality is exact as the definition of the numerical recursion, not as a claim that its finite-gap distribution equals the true OU transition.

10.9 Why a short-time drift does not mean the noise is negligible

Over a small duration hh, a fixed drift rate contributes order hh, while Brownian noise has standard deviation proportional to h\sqrt h. Since h\sqrt h is larger than hh when 0<h<10<h<1, random fluctuations can dominate individual very short increments even though the drift accumulates a systematic effect over time.

This explains why seeing one short movement away from the mean is not evidence against mean reversion. The drift describes a conditional expected tendency embedded in noisier individual changes. Estimation uses many transitions and their time gaps to separate these effects.

The dimensions reinforce the distinction. The return speed θ\theta has units of inverse time, while σ\sigma has units of state divided by square root of time. The quantity θ(μ−Xt)h\theta(\mu-X_t)h and the quantity σhZ\sigma\sqrt h Z both have units of the state, although they scale differently with duration.

10.10 State-dependent diffusion needs an additional integral definition

A general Itô SDE is written

dXt=a(Xt,t)dt+b(Xt,t)dBt. dX_t=a(X_t,t)\,dt+b(X_t,t)\,dB_t.

Its meaning is

Xt=X0+∫0ta(Xs,s)ds+∫0tb(Xs,s)dBs. X_t=X_0+\int_0^t a(X_s,s)\,ds+\int_0^t b(X_s,s)\,dB_s.

Now the Brownian weight can change with the random state. The weighted increment sum no longer telescopes. An Itô integral uses suitable nonanticipating approximations, typically left-endpoint values, and a probabilistic limit. Different integral conventions can differ when the integrand is random and varies with the driving noise.

For the OU model, the original diffusion coefficient is constant. Its explicit solution will involve nonconstant but deterministic exponential weights. That restricted stochastic-integral theory is enough for our derivation and will be developed in Chapter 11. We do not need to assume general nonlinear Itô calculus just to solve this linear additive-noise model.

10.11 Meaning, existence, and uniqueness are separate claims

Writing an integral equation specifies what a solution would have to satisfy. It does not automatically prove that a solution exists or is unique for every choice of coefficients.

One useful sufficient condition in general SDE theory is a Lipschitz condition: the coefficients do not change faster than a fixed multiple of the change in state. For the OU drift,

|θ(μ−x)−θ(μ−y)|=θ|x−y|. |\theta(\mu-x)-\theta(\mu-y)|=\theta|x-y|.

The constant diffusion has zero difference between states. The coefficients also have at most linear growth. These properties place OU within standard existence-and-uniqueness results, under the usual initial-data conditions. More concretely, Chapter 12 constructs the solution and proves uniqueness directly for this model, so its solvability will not rest on an unexplained general theorem.

Worked check. For dXt=(2t+1)dt+3dBtdX_t=(2t+1)dt+3dB_t and X0=4X_0=4, the integral form is Xt=4+∫0t(2s+1)ds+3Bt=4+t2+t+3BtX_t=4+\int_0^t(2s+1)ds+3B_t=4+t^2+t+3B_t. Therefore Xt∼N(4+t2+t,9t)X_t\sim N(4+t^2+t,9t). Replacing the drift by 2−Xt2-X_t would prevent this direct substitution because the unknown process would then appear inside the time integral. The problem would still be meaningful, but it would require solving a self-consistent equation.

Source connection: the integral interpretation of SDEs is discussed in MIT Lecture 21 and Särkkä and Solin, Chapter 4. The examples and exact-versus-Euler distinction are developed here from the integral equations.

11. Weight the noise: the deterministic Wiener integral

IN THIS CHAPTER

  3. 11.3 Derive the mean and variance of the finite sum
  4. 11.4 Comparing two integrals explains how limits will work
  5. 11.5 What “square-integrable” and “mean-square convergence” mean
  6. 11.6 Construct the integral for a general deterministic weight
  7. 11.7 Why the limiting integral is still Gaussian
  8. 11.8 A special integration-by-parts formula requires no Brownian derivative
  9. 11.9 Two smooth examples, worked all the way through
  10. 11.10 What fails when the weight itself is random?
  11. 11.11 A complete covariance example

11.1 What object are we trying to define?

A Brownian motion BtB_t starts at zero and has independent Gaussian increments: over a time interval of length hh, the increment is distributed as N(0,h)N(0,h). Here and throughout these notes, the second argument of N(m,v)N(m,v) is the variance. An increment is the change Bt+h−BtB_{t+h}-B_t, not the value Bt+hB_{t+h} by itself.

Suppose disturbances arriving at different times do not have equal influence on a final outcome. Perhaps an early disturbance has mostly worn off, whereas a recent disturbance is still strongly felt. We need an accumulated-noise model that can assign different weights to different time intervals. The notation for that object is

I(f)=∫abf(s)dBs. I(f)=\int_a^b f(s)\,dB_s.

The function ff specifies the weights. In this chapter it is deterministic: once we choose the function and the interval, its values are fixed, not selected by looking at the realized Brownian path. The resulting integral is nevertheless random because the Brownian increments are random.

For comparison, ∫abf(s)ds\int_a^b f(s)\,ds weights small amounts of time. The integral ∫abf(s)dBs\int_a^b f(s)\,dB_s weights small changes in Brownian motion. Replacing dBsdB_s by dsds changes the object and generally produces the wrong answer.

We will not define this integral as an antiderivative of a nonexistent ordinary Brownian derivative. We will first define it for weights that are constant on a finite collection of intervals. Then we will explain precisely how to take limits to obtain more general deterministic weights.

11.2 Start with weights that are constant on each interval

Choose a partition

a=u0<u1<⋯<um=b. a=u_0<u_1<\cdots<u_m=b.

A partition is simply a list of increasing times dividing the interval into smaller intervals. Let ff equal the constant cjc_j on (uj,uj+1](u_j,u_{j+1}]. Such an ff is called a step function. It can be written compactly as

f(s)=∑j=0m−1cj𝟏(uj,uj+1](s), f(s)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}c_j\mathbf 1_{(u_j,u_{j+1}]}(s),

where the indicator 𝟏A(s)\mathbf 1_A(s) is 1 when ss belongs to the set AA, and 0 otherwise. The indicator notation is only a way to express “use weight cjc_j on the jjth interval.”

For this function, define the integral by the finite sum

I(f)=∑j=0m−1cj(Buj+1−Buj). \boxed{I(f)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}c_j(B_{u_{j+1}}-B_{u_j}).}

There is nothing limiting or informal in this definition. Every Brownian value exists, so every difference and the finite weighted sum exist.

For example, take a=0a=0, b=3b=3, and use weight 2 for the first unit of time and weight −1-1 for the next two units. Then

f(s)={2,0<s≤1,−1,1<s≤3,I(f)=2(B1−B0)−(B3−B1). f(s)=\begin{cases}2,&0<s\leq1,\\-1,&1<s\leq3,\end{cases} \qquad I(f)=2(B_1-B_0)-(B_3-B_1).

Because B0=0B_0=0, this equals 2B1−(B3−B1)2B_1-(B_3-B_1). A negative weight reverses the sign of a disturbance; it does not make its variance negative.

11.3 Derive the mean and variance of the finite sum

Write ΔBj=Buj+1−Buj\Delta B_j=B_{u_{j+1}}-B_{u_j} and hj=uj+1−ujh_j=u_{j+1}-u_j. Brownian motion gives E[ΔBj]=0E[\Delta B_j]=0, E[(ΔBj)2]=hjE[(\Delta B_j)^2]=h_j, and independence between increments from distinct intervals.

Linearity of expectation therefore gives

E[I(f)]=∑jcjE[ΔBj]=0. E[I(f)]=\sum_j c_j E[\Delta B_j]=0.

Since the mean is zero, the variance equals the second moment. Expand the square before taking its expectation:

I(f)2=∑jcj2(ΔBj)2+2∑j<kcjckΔBjΔBk. I(f)^2 =\sum_j c_j^2(\Delta B_j)^2 +2\sum_{j<k}c_jc_k\Delta B_j\Delta B_k.

For j≠kj\ne k, independence permits multiplication of the expectations:

E[ΔBjΔBk]=E[ΔBj]E[ΔBk]=0. E[\Delta B_j\Delta B_k] =E[\Delta B_j]E[\Delta B_k]=0.

Consequently every cross term disappears, while each diagonal term contributes its interval length:

Var(I(f))=∑jcj2E[(ΔBj)2]=∑jcj2hj=∫abf(s)2ds. \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(I(f)) &=\sum_j c_j^2 E[(\Delta B_j)^2]\\ &=\sum_j c_j^2h_j\\ &=\int_a^b f(s)^2\,ds. \end{aligned}

The last equality is an ordinary integral of a step function: its value is the sum of rectangle heights cj2c_j^2 multiplied by their widths hjh_j.

For our two-weight example, the variance is 22(1)+(−1)2(2)=62^2(1)+(-1)^2(2)=6. The two coefficients must be squared individually. Neither ∫f(s)ds\int f(s)\,ds nor (∫f(s)ds)2(\int f(s)\,ds)^2 is the variance. In fact, this example has ∫03f(s)ds=2−2=0\int_0^3 f(s)\,ds=2-2=0 even though the random integral has variance 6. Opposite weights cancel in the ordinary integral; independent random disturbances do not cancel deterministically.

Each summand is Gaussian, and a sum of independent Gaussian variables is Gaussian. Therefore the finite-sum definition gives the exact law

I(f)∼N(0,∫abf(s)2ds). I(f)\sim N\!\left(0,\int_a^b f(s)^2\,ds\right).

This is not an appeal to a central limit theorem. Even two weighted independent Brownian increments already give an exactly Gaussian sum.

11.4 Comparing two integrals explains how limits will work

Suppose ff and gg are step functions. Their breakpoints may differ, but we can combine both sets of breakpoints into a common partition. On each resulting interval, write their weights as cjc_j and djd_j.

The finite sums show directly that

I(αf+βg)=αI(f)+βI(g) I(\alpha f+\beta g)=\alpha I(f)+\beta I(g)

for deterministic numbers α,β\alpha,\beta. This property is called linearity. It follows because each Brownian increment is multiplied by αcj+βdj\alpha c_j+\beta d_j, and distributing that multiplication separates the sums.

They also give a covariance identity. Both integrals have mean zero, so

Cov(I(f),I(g))=E[(∑jcjΔBj)(∑kdkΔBk)]=∑j∑kcjdkE[ΔBjΔBk]=∑jcjdjhj=∫abf(s)g(s)ds. \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(I(f),I(g)) &=E\!\left[\left(\sum_j c_j\Delta B_j\right) \left(\sum_k d_k\Delta B_k\right)\right]\\ &=\sum_j\sum_k c_jd_kE[\Delta B_j\Delta B_k]\\ &=\sum_j c_jd_jh_j\\ &=\int_a^b f(s)g(s)\,ds. \end{aligned}

As before, different increments contribute zero cross expectation. Only the same-interval pairs survive.

Apply the variance formula to f−gf-g. By linearity, its integral is I(f)−I(g)I(f)-I(g), and hence

E[(I(f)−I(g))2]=∫ab(f(s)−g(s))2ds. \boxed{E[(I(f)-I(g))^2]=\int_a^b(f(s)-g(s))^2\,ds.}

This is the crucial bridge. It says that a small integrated squared error in the weights produces an equally small expected squared error in the random integrals. That is the control needed to define integrals by approximation.

11.5 What “square-integrable” and “mean-square convergence” mean

A deterministic function ff is square-integrable on [a,b][a,b] when

∫ab|f(s)|2ds<∞. \int_a^b|f(s)|^2\,ds<\infty.

The collection of such functions is conventionally called L2([a,b])L^2([a,b]). The notation L2L^2 is not another stochastic model; it describes a class of functions with a finite squared-integral size. Functions that differ only on a set of time length zero represent the same element for this purpose.

For the smooth functions used later, such as exponentials on finite intervals, square-integrability is immediate: a bounded function on a finite interval has a finite integral of its square. More singular functions can also qualify. For example, f(s)=s−1/4f(s)=s^{-1/4} on (0,1](0,1] has ∫01f(s)2ds=∫01s−1/2ds=2\int_0^1f(s)^2ds=\int_0^1s^{-1/2}ds=2. In contrast, s−1/2s^{-1/2} on (0,1](0,1] does not qualify because its square has divergent integral ∫01s−1ds\int_0^1s^{-1}ds.

A sequence of random variables UmU_m converges to UU in mean square when

E[(Um−U)2]→0. E[(U_m-U)^2]\longrightarrow0.

This is a statement about the average squared discrepancy across random outcomes. It does not mean every approximation equals the limit, nor does it automatically assert convergence along every individual path.

Mean-square convergence implies convergence in probability. Indeed, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0,

P(|Um−U|>ε)≤E[(Um−U)2]ε2→0. P(|U_m-U|>\varepsilon) \leq\frac{E[(U_m-U)^2]}{\varepsilon^2}\longrightarrow0.

The inequality follows because on the event |Um−U|>ε|U_m-U|>\varepsilon, the squared error is at least ε2\varepsilon^2. This elementary argument also explains why expected squared error is a useful way to control approximation.

11.6 Construct the integral for a general deterministic weight

Take a deterministic square-integrable ff. A standard approximation theorem says that step functions fmf_m can be chosen with

∫ab(fm(s)−f(s))2ds→0. \int_a^b(f_m(s)-f(s))^2\,ds\longrightarrow0.

For continuous ff, taking its values on increasingly fine partitions gives an intuitive construction. The approximation theorem extends the statement to all square-integrable ff; we use that functional-analysis result rather than prove it here.

We already know how to define each I(fm)I(f_m). The difference identity gives

E[(I(fm)−I(fk))2]=∫ab(fm−fk)2ds→0as m,k→∞. E[(I(f_m)-I(f_k))^2]=\int_a^b(f_m-f_k)^2\,ds\longrightarrow0 \quad\text{as }m,k\to\infty.

Thus the random integrals form a Cauchy sequence in mean square: late members become arbitrarily close to one another in expected squared error. Completeness of the space of square-integrable random variables guarantees a mean-square limit. Completeness is the general mathematical theorem that “Cauchy sequences in this space have a limit in the same space.”

We define I(f)I(f) to be this limit. There is still a question: would a different sequence of step approximations produce another integral? Let gmg_m also approximate ff in squared-integral norm. Then

E[(I(fm)−I(gm))2]=∫ab(fm−gm)2ds→0. E[(I(f_m)-I(g_m))^2]=\int_a^b(f_m-g_m)^2\,ds\longrightarrow0.

Therefore their limits agree in mean square and hence almost surely. The integral does not depend on which valid approximation sequence we chose. This uniqueness is essential: otherwise the symbol ∫fdB\int f\,dB would not identify a well-defined random variable.

Linearity extends to the limits. The mean remains zero because

|E[I(fm)]−E[I(f)]|≤E[|I(fm)−I(f)|]≤E[(I(fm)−I(f))2]→0. |E[I(f_m)]-E[I(f)]| \leq E[|I(f_m)-I(f)|] \leq\sqrt{E[(I(f_m)-I(f))^2]}\longrightarrow0.

The second inequality is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality applied to the random error and the constant 1. The finite-sum second-moment identity extends as well:

E[(∫abf(s)dBs)2]=∫abf(s)2ds. \boxed{E\!\left[\left(\int_a^bf(s)\,dB_s\right)^2\right] =\int_a^bf(s)^2\,ds.}

This is the Itô isometry, here in its deterministic-integrand form. An isometry preserves a notion of size or distance. The preceding difference identity explains the name more fully: squared-integral distance between deterministic functions becomes mean-square distance between their stochastic integrals.

11.7 Why the limiting integral is still Gaussian

Knowing the mean and variance of a random variable does not generally determine its distribution. We therefore need to justify the additional Gaussian conclusion, rather than infer it just from the isometry.

Each approximating integral has distribution N(0,vm)N(0,v_m), where vm=∫fm2v_m=\int f_m^2. Squared-integral convergence of fmf_m to ff implies vm→v=∫f2v_m\to v=\int f^2. For example, using Cauchy–Schwarz,

|∫(fm2−f2)|=|∫(fm−f)(fm+f)|≤(∫(fm−f)2)1/2(∫(fm+f)2)1/2→0. \left|\int(f_m^2-f^2)\right| =\left|\int(f_m-f)(f_m+f)\right| \leq\left(\int(f_m-f)^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\int(f_m+f)^2\right)^{1/2}\longrightarrow0.

The first factor tends to zero and the second stays bounded. Thus the Gaussian distributions of the approximations tend to N(0,v)N(0,v). At the same time, mean-square convergence makes I(fm)I(f_m) converge in probability, and therefore in distribution, to I(f)I(f). Uniqueness of the limiting distribution gives

∫abf(s)dBs∼N(0,∫abf(s)2ds). \boxed{\int_a^bf(s)\,dB_s\sim N\!\left(0,\int_a^bf(s)^2\,ds\right).}

Here we use the standard facts that probability convergence implies distribution convergence and that a distributional limit is unique. The argument is specific: Gaussian approximations whose variances converge, not an assertion that every limit of arbitrary weighted noise must be Gaussian. When v=0v=0, the integral is zero almost surely, conventionally a degenerate Gaussian.

The covariance identity also extends:

Cov(∫fdB,∫gdB)=∫fg. \operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\int f\,dB,\int g\,dB\right)=\int fg.

Moreover, any finite collection of these deterministic-weight integrals is jointly Gaussian. To see why, any linear combination is the integral of the corresponding linear combination of deterministic weights, so it is Gaussian. This is one characterization of a jointly Gaussian vector.

For jointly Gaussian variables, zero covariance implies independence. Consequently, deterministic-weight integrals over disjoint intervals are independent: their weights have disjoint supports, so fg=0fg=0 except possibly at endpoints, and the covariance integral is zero. An integral over (s,t](s,t] is also independent of the Brownian information up to time ss. Its approximating sums use only future independent increments. If an initial value X0X_0 is independent of future Brownian noise, adding that initial value to the past information preserves this conclusion.

11.8 A special integration-by-parts formula requires no Brownian derivative

For a deterministic continuously differentiable ff, the Wiener integral can also be written using an ordinary time integral of the Brownian path. This is especially useful for solving OU without invoking the full stochastic product rule.

Begin with the exact finite-partition identity

f(uj+1)Buj+1−f(uj)Buj=f(uj)(Buj+1−Buj)+Buj+1(f(uj+1)−f(uj)). \begin{aligned} f(u_{j+1})B_{u_{j+1}}-f(u_j)B_{u_j} ={}&f(u_j)(B_{u_{j+1}}-B_{u_j})\\ &+B_{u_{j+1}}(f(u_{j+1})-f(u_j)). \end{aligned}

Check it by expanding the right side: the two terms involving f(uj)Buj+1f(u_j)B_{u_{j+1}} cancel. Sum over all intervals. The left side telescopes, leaving only endpoint products. Rearranging gives

∑jf(uj)(Buj+1−Buj)=f(b)Bb−f(a)Ba−∑jBuj+1(f(uj+1)−f(uj)). \begin{aligned} \sum_j f(u_j)(B_{u_{j+1}}-B_{u_j}) ={}&f(b)B_b-f(a)B_a\\ &-\sum_j B_{u_{j+1}}(f(u_{j+1})-f(u_j)). \end{aligned}

As the partition becomes fine, the first sum on the left converges in mean square to the Wiener integral, because the left-step approximations converge to the continuous ff. On the right, use

f(uj+1)−f(uj)=∫ujuj+1f′(s)ds. f(u_{j+1})-f(u_j)=\int_{u_j}^{u_{j+1}}f'(s)\,ds.

Continuity of the Brownian path ensures that replacing Buj+1B_{u_{j+1}} by BsB_s within these small intervals changes the sum by a quantity tending to zero. More explicitly, its absolute error is at most the maximum within-interval oscillation of BB multiplied by ∫ab|f′(s)|ds\int_a^b|f'(s)|ds. Uniform continuity on the finite interval makes that maximum oscillation tend to zero almost surely.

Thus the right side has a pathwise limit. Since the left side also has a mean-square limit, both limits agree almost surely. We obtain

∫abf(s)dBs=f(b)Bb−f(a)Ba−∫abf′(s)Bsds. \boxed{\int_a^bf(s)\,dB_s =f(b)B_b-f(a)B_a-\int_a^bf'(s)B_s\,ds.}

The derivative in this formula is f′f', not B′B'. Brownian motion appears inside an ordinary integral as a continuous function. This is why the calculation is legal despite Brownian paths having no ordinary derivative.

11.9 Two smooth examples, worked all the way through

First use f(s)=sf(s)=s on [0,t][0,t]. The Gaussian law and the isometry give

E[∫0tsdBs]=0,Var(∫0tsdBs)=∫0ts2ds=[s33]0t=t33. E\!\left[\int_0^t s\,dB_s\right]=0, \qquad \operatorname{Var}\!\left(\int_0^t s\,dB_s\right) =\int_0^t s^2ds =\left[\frac{s^3}{3}\right]_0^t=\frac{t^3}{3}.

Therefore ∫0tsdBs∼N(0,t3/3)\int_0^t s\,dB_s\sim N(0,t^3/3). Independently, the integration-by-parts formula, with f′(s)=1f'(s)=1, gives

∫0tsdBs=tBt−∫0tBsds. \int_0^t s\,dB_s=tB_t-\int_0^t B_s\,ds.

These are two descriptions of the same random variable: one gives its distribution, and one expresses it in terms of a realized path. The ordinary integral on the right remains random because its integrand is the random path.

Now fix a terminal time tt and a positive number θ\theta, and use f(s)=e−θ(t−s)f(s)=e^{-\theta(t-s)}. Even though the symbol tt appears in the weight, the weight is deterministic once the terminal time is fixed. Its derivative with respect to the integration variable ss is

f′(s)=θe−θ(t−s). f'(s)=\theta e^{-\theta(t-s)}.

The sign is positive: −θ(t−s)=−θt+θs-\theta(t-s)=-\theta t+\theta s. Integration by parts gives

∫0te−θ(t−s)dBs=Bt−θ∫0te−θ(t−s)Bsds. \boxed{\int_0^t e^{-\theta(t-s)}\,dB_s =B_t-\theta\int_0^t e^{-\theta(t-s)}B_s\,ds.}

The variance follows by squaring the weight, substituting r=t−sr=t-s, and integrating:

∫0te−2θ(t−s)ds=∫0te−2θrdr=[−e−2θr2θ]0t=1−e−2θt2θ. \begin{aligned} \int_0^t e^{-2\theta(t-s)}ds &=\int_0^t e^{-2\theta r}dr\\ &=\left[-\frac{e^{-2\theta r}}{2\theta}\right]_0^t\\ &=\frac{1-e^{-2\theta t}}{2\theta}. \end{aligned}

Both the pathwise identity and this variance calculation will be used in the OU solution.

11.10 What fails when the weight itself is random?

The deterministic restriction is substantive. A random weight may depend on the same noise that appears in the increment sum, so the finite sum is no longer a fixed linear combination of independent Gaussian variables. A general adapted Itô integral can still exist and satisfy a suitable isometry, but its distribution need not be Gaussian.

A concrete illustration is the random integrand BsB_s itself. On a partition, the elementary identity

Buj+12−Buj2=2Buj(Buj+1−Buj)+(Buj+1−Buj)2 B_{u_{j+1}}^2-B_{u_j}^2 =2B_{u_j}(B_{u_{j+1}}-B_{u_j}) +(B_{u_{j+1}}-B_{u_j})^2

gives, after summing and using B0=0B_0=0,

∑jBujΔBj=12(Bt2−∑j(ΔBj)2). \sum_jB_{u_j}\Delta B_j =\frac12\left(B_t^2-\sum_j(\Delta B_j)^2\right).

For Brownian motion the sum of squared increments tends to tt in mean square as a deterministic partition’s mesh tends to zero. The reason is that its mean is ∑jhj=t\sum_jh_j=t and its variance is 2∑jhj2≤2tmaxjhj→02\sum_jh_j^2\leq2t\max_jh_j\to0. Thus the left-endpoint sums here converge to

∫0tBsdBs=12(Bt2−t). \int_0^tB_s\,dB_s=\frac12(B_t^2-t).

For t>0t>0, this is not a Gaussian random variable: it is nonconstant but can never be less than −t/2-t/2, whereas any nondegenerate Gaussian has possible values arbitrarily far in both directions. The example is not a construction of every random-integrand integral. It is a direct counterexample to the idea that “integrating against Brownian motion always produces a Gaussian.”

11.11 A complete covariance example

Let f=2f=2 on (0,1](0,1] and f=−1f=-1 on (1,3](1,3]. Let g=1g=1 on (0,2](0,2] and g=0g=0 on (2,3](2,3]. Define U=∫03fdBU=\int_0^3f\,dB and V=∫03gdBV=\int_0^3g\,dB.

Use the common partition 0,1,2,30,1,2,3. The weights are (2,−1,−1)(2,-1,-1) for UU and (1,1,0)(1,1,0) for VV, on intervals of unit length. Therefore

Var(U)=4+1+1=6,Var(V)=1+1+0=2, \operatorname{Var}(U)=4+1+1=6, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(V)=1+1+0=2,

and

Cov(U,V)=2(1)+(−1)(1)+(−1)(0)=1. \operatorname{Cov}(U,V)=2(1)+(-1)(1)+(-1)(0)=1.

Thus Corr(U,V)=1/12\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)=1/\sqrt{12}. The pair is jointly Gaussian, but not independent because the covariance is nonzero. Also U+V=∫(f+g)dBU+V=\int(f+g)dB has weights (3,0,−1)(3,0,-1), hence variance 9+0+1=109+0+1=10. This agrees with the general variance formula 6+2+2(1)=106+2+2(1)=10.

The central lesson is now precise. Deterministic weights turn Brownian increments into a Gaussian accumulated noise whose variance is the ordinary integral of the squared weights. We know how the object is constructed, why the construction is independent of the approximations, and why its law has the stated form.

Source connection: deterministic Wiener integration and the Itô isometry are treated in MIT Lecture 18 and Särkkä and Solin, §4.1. The finite-sum proofs, approximation explanation and deterministic integration-by-parts derivation are given explicitly here. The general density of step functions and completeness of the square-integrable spaces are identified as standard theorems, not presented as proofs completed in these notes.

12. Solve the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model

IN THIS CHAPTER

  1. 12.1 State the model and separate the two possible tasks
  2. 12.2 First solve the same return mechanism without noise
  3. 12.3 Remove the rough noise before using ordinary differentiation
  4. 12.4 Solve the transformed ordinary equation step by step
  5. 12.5 Express the solution as a weighted stochastic integral
  6. 12.6 Verify that the construction is a solution and that it is unique
  7. 12.7 Derive the distribution from a fixed starting value
  8. 12.8 Derive the transition from an arbitrary observed time
  9. 12.9 Identify the stationary distribution and explain initialization
  10. 12.10 Derive covariance and correlation, including the fixed-start case
  11. 12.11 Check short gaps, long gaps, half-life and units

12.1 State the model and separate the two possible tasks

The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, or OU process, is defined here by

dXt=θ(μ−Xt)dt+σdBt,θ>0,σ>0,μ∈ℝ. dX_t=\theta(\mu-X_t)\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t, \qquad \theta>0,\quad\sigma>0,\quad\mu\in\mathbb R.

The parameter μ\mu is the level toward which the process tends to return. The positive parameter θ\theta determines the speed of this return. The positive parameter σ\sigma scales the Brownian disturbances. Standard Brownian motion has independent increments Bt+h−Bt∼N(0,h)B_{t+h}-B_t\sim N(0,h), so the noise accumulated over a short interval has standard deviation proportional to h\sqrt h.

There are two different tasks involving these parameters. Solving the model means finding a process XtX_t for specified parameter values, an initial value and Brownian noise. Estimating the model means inferring parameter values from observed process values. This chapter solves the model first. The resulting transition distribution will make estimation possible in Chapter 13.

The differential equation is shorthand for the integral equation

Xt=X0+θ∫0t(μ−Xs)ds+σBt. \boxed{X_t=X_0+\theta\int_0^t(\mu-X_s)\,ds+\sigma B_t.}

Initially take X0=x0X_0=x_0 fixed. We will later allow a random initial value independent of future Brownian increments. The ordinary time integral on the right is well-defined along a continuous path. The challenge is that it contains the unknown XsX_s itself. We want to remove that self-reference.

12.2 First solve the same return mechanism without noise

Ignore the noise temporarily and consider the ordinary equation

x′(t)=θ(μ−x(t)),x(0)=x0. x'(t)=\theta(\mu-x(t)),\qquad x(0)=x_0.

Shift the variable by its target: let y(t)=x(t)−μy(t)=x(t)-\mu. Because μ\mu is a constant, y′(t)=x′(t)y'(t)=x'(t), and the equation becomes

y′(t)=−θy(t). y'(t)=-\theta y(t).

To solve it, multiply by eθte^{\theta t}. Why that factor? The ordinary product rule gives

ddt(eθty(t))=θeθty(t)+eθty′(t)=θeθty(t)−θeθty(t)=0. \begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dt}\big(e^{\theta t}y(t)\big) &=\theta e^{\theta t}y(t)+e^{\theta t}y'(t)\\ &=\theta e^{\theta t}y(t)-\theta e^{\theta t}y(t)\\ &=0. \end{aligned}

The exponential was chosen so that its derivative generates exactly the term needed to cancel the original decay. A function with derivative zero is constant, so eθty(t)=y(0)=x0−μe^{\theta t}y(t)=y(0)=x_0-\mu. Hence

x(t)=μ+e−θt(x0−μ). x(t)=\mu+e^{-\theta t}(x_0-\mu).

The deviation from the target is multiplied by e−θte^{-\theta t}. It becomes smaller as time passes because θ>0\theta>0. We expect this deterministic decay to remain in the stochastic solution, but the noise creates a new issue: XtX_t is not ordinarily differentiable. We must not simply pretend that the same derivative calculation applies to the entire noisy process without justification.

12.3 Remove the rough noise before using ordinary differentiation

Center the stochastic process in the same way:

Yt=Xt−μ. Y_t=X_t-\mu.

The integral equation becomes

Yt=Y0−θ∫0tYsds+σBt. Y_t=Y_0-\theta\int_0^tY_s\,ds+\sigma B_t.

Now introduce a second process

Vt=Yt−σBt. V_t=Y_t-\sigma B_t.

This subtraction is useful because it removes the explicitly rough Brownian contribution. Substituting Ys=Vs+σBsY_s=V_s+\sigma B_s into the integral equation gives

Vt=Y0−θ∫0t(Vs+σBs)ds. V_t=Y_0-\theta\int_0^t\big(V_s+\sigma B_s\big)\,ds.

For any fixed continuous Brownian path, the right side is an ordinary integral of a continuous function. Therefore VtV_t is ordinarily differentiable along that path, even though YtY_t need not be. Differentiating this ordinary integral equation is legitimate and yields

V′(t)=−θVt−θσBt,V0=Y0. V'(t)=-\theta V_t-\theta\sigma B_t, \qquad V_0=Y_0.

Notice what has not happened: we have not differentiated BtB_t. It is merely a continuous forcing term on the right of an ordinary differential equation. An equation can be driven by a nondifferentiable continuous input and still have a differentiable accumulated response.

This converts the stochastic problem into an ordinary linear equation with a random but fixed-in-the-calculation input path. We can now apply the integrating-factor method without treating Brownian motion as differentiable.

12.4 Solve the transformed ordinary equation step by step

Multiply the equation for VV by eθte^{\theta t} and apply the ordinary product rule:

ddt(eθtVt)=eθt(V′(t)+θVt)=−θσeθtBt. \begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dt}\big(e^{\theta t}V_t\big) &=e^{\theta t}\big(V'(t)+\theta V_t\big)\\ &=-\theta\sigma e^{\theta t}B_t. \end{aligned}

Integrate from 0 to tt:

eθtVt−V0=−θσ∫0teθsBsds. e^{\theta t}V_t-V_0 =-\theta\sigma\int_0^t e^{\theta s}B_s\,ds.

Since V0=Y0V_0=Y_0, dividing by eθte^{\theta t} gives

Vt=e−θtY0−θσ∫0te−θ(t−s)Bsds. V_t=e^{-\theta t}Y_0 -\theta\sigma\int_0^t e^{-\theta(t-s)}B_s\,ds.

Finally recover Yt=Vt+σBtY_t=V_t+\sigma B_t and then Xt=μ+YtX_t=\mu+Y_t:

Xt=μ+e−θt(X0−μ)+σ[Bt−θ∫0te−θ(t−s)Bsds]. \boxed{ X_t=\mu+e^{-\theta t}(X_0-\mu) +\sigma\left[B_t-\theta\int_0^t e^{-\theta(t-s)}B_s\,ds\right].}

Everything in this expression is already defined using Brownian values and an ordinary time integral. It is an explicit solution: the unknown process no longer appears inside its own integral. This formula is also a direct construction of a continuous process, because BB and the ordinary integral term are continuous.

12.5 Express the solution as a weighted stochastic integral

The usual OU solution is written in a more interpretable weighted-noise form. For a deterministic continuously differentiable ff, integration by parts against Brownian motion gives

∫0tf(s)dBs=f(t)Bt−f(0)B0−∫0tf′(s)Bsds. \int_0^tf(s)\,dB_s=f(t)B_t-f(0)B_0-\int_0^tf'(s)B_s\,ds.

This identity does not require B′B': it follows from a finite telescoping product identity and continuity, as derived in Chapter 11. In the present calculation take f(s)=e−θ(t−s)f(s)=e^{-\theta(t-s)}, treating the terminal time tt as fixed. Then f(t)=1f(t)=1, B0=0B_0=0, and f′(s)=θe−θ(t−s)f'(s)=\theta e^{-\theta(t-s)}. Hence

Bt−θ∫0te−θ(t−s)Bsds=∫0te−θ(t−s)dBs. B_t-\theta\int_0^t e^{-\theta(t-s)}B_s\,ds =\int_0^t e^{-\theta(t-s)}\,dB_s.

Substitute this into the explicit pathwise solution:

Xt=μ+e−θt(X0−μ)+σ∫0te−θ(t−s)dBs. \boxed{ X_t=\mu+e^{-\theta t}(X_0-\mu) +\sigma\int_0^t e^{-\theta(t-s)}\,dB_s.}

The first term is the target level. The second is the surviving part of the initial deviation. The third is all the later noise, with each disturbance damped according to its age. A disturbance arriving near s=ts=t has weight close to 1. A disturbance arriving long before tt has a smaller weight e−θ(t−s)e^{-\theta(t-s)}.

This is the continuous-time version of an AR(1) expansion in which old innovations carry powers of an autoregressive coefficient. The exponential weight is not guessed solely from analogy: we derived it from the equation.

12.6 Verify that the construction is a solution and that it is unique

The ordinary equation for VV supplies a short verification. Define VV by the explicit expression in §12.4. Ordinary differentiation shows it satisfies

V′(t)=−θ(Vt+σBt),V0=X0−μ. V'(t)=-\theta(V_t+\sigma B_t),\qquad V_0=X_0-\mu.

Integrating this equation and defining Xt=μ+Vt+σBtX_t=\mu+V_t+\sigma B_t gives

Xt=μ+V0−θ∫0t(Vs+σBs)ds+σBt=X0−θ∫0t(Xs−μ)ds+σBt=X0+θ∫0t(μ−Xs)ds+σBt. \begin{aligned} X_t &=\mu+V_0-\theta\int_0^t(V_s+\sigma B_s)ds+\sigma B_t\\ &=X_0-\theta\int_0^t(X_s-\mu)ds+\sigma B_t\\ &=X_0+\theta\int_0^t(\mu-X_s)ds+\sigma B_t. \end{aligned}

That is exactly the defining integral equation. No approximation has been used.

For uniqueness, suppose XX and X̃\widetilde X are continuous solutions with the same initial value and the same Brownian path. Their difference Dt=Xt−X̃tD_t=X_t-\widetilde X_t satisfies

Dt=−θ∫0tDsds. D_t=-\theta\int_0^tD_s\,ds.

The Brownian terms cancel. This difference is therefore differentiable, with D′(t)=−θDtD'(t)=-\theta D_t and D0=0D_0=0. The ordinary solution from §12.2 is Dt=e−θtD0=0D_t=e^{-\theta t}D_0=0. Thus the solutions agree at all times along the continuous path.

Different Brownian paths produce different OU paths; uniqueness does not say every realization looks the same. It says that once the initial value and driving noise are fixed, the model does not leave multiple possible responses.

12.7 Derive the distribution from a fixed starting value

Let X0=x0X_0=x_0 be fixed. A deterministic weighted Brownian integral is a centered Gaussian, with variance equal to the ordinary integral of the squared weight. Consequently, the random term

Zt=σ∫0te−θ(t−s)dBs Z_t=\sigma\int_0^t e^{-\theta(t-s)}\,dB_s

has mean zero. Its variance is

Var(Zt)=σ2∫0te−2θ(t−s)ds=σ2∫0te−2θrdr(r=t−s)=σ2[−e−2θr2θ]0t=σ22θ(1−e−2θt). \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(Z_t) &=\sigma^2\int_0^t e^{-2\theta(t-s)}\,ds\\ &=\sigma^2\int_0^t e^{-2\theta r}\,dr \qquad(r=t-s)\\ &=\sigma^2\left[-\frac{e^{-2\theta r}}{2\theta}\right]_0^t\\ &=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}(1-e^{-2\theta t}). \end{aligned}

The factor 2θ2\theta appears because the exponential weight was squared in the variance calculation. Taking the expectation of the solution removes only its centered random term:

E[Xt∣X0=x0]=μ+e−θt(x0−μ). E[X_t\mid X_0=x_0]=\mu+e^{-\theta t}(x_0-\mu).

Adding a deterministic number to a Gaussian shifts its mean without changing its variance. Therefore

Xt∣X0=x0∼N(μ+e−θt(x0−μ),σ22θ(1−e−2θt)). \boxed{ X_t\mid X_0=x_0 \sim N\!\left( \mu+e^{-\theta t}(x_0-\mu), \frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}(1-e^{-2\theta t}) \right).}

At t=0t=0, the conditional variance is zero because the starting value is known. For any t>0t>0, the variance is positive. Mean reversion controls the accumulation of noise; it does not eliminate noise.

12.8 Derive the transition from an arbitrary observed time

To use data, we need the distribution of XtX_t given an earlier value XsX_s, not only a distribution from time zero. Split the noise integral in the solution at time s<ts<t:

∫0te−θ(t−u)dBu=∫0se−θ(t−u)dBu+∫ste−θ(t−u)dBu. \int_0^t e^{-\theta(t-u)}dB_u =\int_0^s e^{-\theta(t-u)}dB_u +\int_s^t e^{-\theta(t-u)}dB_u.

For u≤su\leq s, the exponential factors as

e−θ(t−u)=e−θ(t−s)e−θ(s−u). e^{-\theta(t-u)}=e^{-\theta(t-s)}e^{-\theta(s-u)}.

Therefore the portion containing the initial value and all noise before ss is

e−θt(X0−μ)+σ∫0se−θ(t−u)dBu=e−θ(t−s)[e−θs(X0−μ)+σ∫0se−θ(s−u)dBu]=e−θ(t−s)(Xs−μ). \begin{aligned} &e^{-\theta t}(X_0-\mu) +\sigma\int_0^s e^{-\theta(t-u)}dB_u\\ &\qquad=e^{-\theta(t-s)} \left[e^{-\theta s}(X_0-\mu) +\sigma\int_0^s e^{-\theta(s-u)}dB_u\right]\\ &\qquad=e^{-\theta(t-s)}(X_s-\mu). \end{aligned}

Substitution yields the exact restart relation

Xt=μ+e−θ(t−s)(Xs−μ)+σ∫ste−θ(t−u)dBu. \boxed{X_t=\mu+e^{-\theta(t-s)}(X_s-\mu) +\sigma\int_s^t e^{-\theta(t-u)}dB_u.}

The final integral depends only on Brownian increments after ss. Its deterministic weight makes it Gaussian, and independent increments make it independent of the information available by ss, including an independent initial value. Once XsX_s is supplied, the earlier path adds no further information to this conditional distribution. This is the Markov property, now justified by the solution rather than assumed without explanation.

Write Δ=t−s>0\Delta=t-s>0 and suppose Xs=xX_s=x. The conditional distribution is

Xs+Δ∣Xs=x∼N(mΔ(x),vΔ), \boxed{ X_{s+\Delta}\mid X_s=x \sim N\big(m_\Delta(x),v_\Delta\big),}

where

mΔ(x)=μ+e−θΔ(x−μ),vΔ=σ22θ(1−e−2θΔ). m_\Delta(x)=\mu+e^{-\theta\Delta}(x-\mu), \qquad v_\Delta=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}(1-e^{-2\theta\Delta}).

The transition depends on the elapsed duration Δ\Delta, not the calendar time ss. That is time-homogeneity in continuous time. It does not require every pair of recorded observations to have the same gap.

12.9 Identify the stationary distribution and explain initialization

Define

q=σ22θ. q=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}.

This is a convenient name for a variance, not an extra independent parameter. For a fixed starting value, as t→∞t\to\infty, the mean tends to μ\mu and the variance tends to qq. The Gaussian distributions therefore approach N(μ,q)N(\mu,q).

To check that this is an invariant distribution, suppose the current value is already distributed as N(μ,q)N(\mu,q) and is independent of future noise. Set ϕ=e−θΔ\phi=e^{-\theta\Delta}. The transition can be expressed as

Xs+Δ=μ+ϕ(Xs−μ)+ε,ε∼N(0,q(1−ϕ2)), X_{s+\Delta}=\mu+\phi(X_s-\mu)+\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon\sim N(0,q(1-\phi^2)),

with ε\varepsilon independent of XsX_s. The next value is Gaussian, its mean is μ\mu, and its variance is

ϕ2q+q(1−ϕ2)=q. \phi^2q+q(1-\phi^2)=q.

Thus the transition preserves N(μ,q)N(\mu,q) for every positive duration. Starting with

X0∼N(μ,q) X_0\sim N(\mu,q)

independently of future Brownian increments gives a stationary OU process. Its joint laws are invariant under time shifts because the initial marginal is invariant and all subsequent conditional laws depend only on elapsed gaps.

Starting at a fixed x0x_0 gives a different situation. Its variance begins at zero and increases toward qq, so that process is not stationary from the start. Also, convergence of distributions to a stationary law does not say an individual path settles permanently at μ\mu. In stationarity there is still positive variance and continuing random movement.

More generally, for an independent random initial value with finite mean m0m_0 and variance v0v_0, the solution gives

E[Xt]=μ+e−θt(m0−μ), E[X_t]=\mu+e^{-\theta t}(m_0-\mu),

and, because the initial value and future noise are independent,

Var(Xt)=e−2θtv0+q(1−e−2θt). \operatorname{Var}(X_t) =e^{-2\theta t}v_0+q(1-e^{-2\theta t}).

Setting m0=μm_0=\mu and v0=qv_0=q makes these moments time-invariant. To conclude Gaussian stationarity from the initialization argument above, take the Gaussian initial distribution, not merely an arbitrary initial distribution with those two moments.

12.10 Derive covariance and correlation, including the fixed-start case

For s≤ts\leq t, use the restart relation and take covariance with XsX_s:

Cov(Xs,Xt)=Cov(Xs,μ+e−θ(t−s)(Xs−μ)+future noise)=e−θ(t−s)Var(Xs). \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(X_s,X_t) &=\operatorname{Cov}\big(X_s,\mu+e^{-\theta(t-s)}(X_s-\mu) +\text{future noise}\big)\\ &=e^{-\theta(t-s)}\operatorname{Var}(X_s). \end{aligned}

Constants contribute zero covariance, and the future noise is independent of XsX_s. In stationarity, Var(Xs)=q\operatorname{Var}(X_s)=q, so

Cov(Xs,Xt)=qe−θ|t−s|. \boxed{\operatorname{Cov}(X_s,X_t)=q e^{-\theta|t-s|}.}

Both standard deviations are q\sqrt q. Dividing covariance by their product gives

Corr(Xs,Xt)=e−θ|t−s|. \boxed{\operatorname{Corr}(X_s,X_t)=e^{-\theta|t-s|}.}

The same exponential controls how much a current deviation survives in a future forecast and how strongly two stationary values are correlated.

For a fixed initial value, use Var(Xs)=q(1−e−2θs)\operatorname{Var}(X_s)=q(1-e^{-2\theta s}) instead. For s≤ts\leq t,

Cov(Xs,Xt)=qe−θ(t−s)(1−e−2θs)=q(e−θ(t−s)−e−θ(t+s)). \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(X_s,X_t) &=q e^{-\theta(t-s)}(1-e^{-2\theta s})\\ &=q\big(e^{-\theta(t-s)}-e^{-\theta(t+s)}\big). \end{aligned}

The symmetric form is q(e−θ|t−s|−e−θ(t+s))q(e^{-\theta|t-s|}-e^{-\theta(t+s)}). It depends on the two times separately, not just their difference. This is a direct mathematical indication that the fixed-start process is not stationary. At time zero the value has zero variance, so its correlation with a later value is undefined even though its covariance is zero.

12.11 Check short gaps, long gaps, half-life and units

For small Δ\Delta, use the first terms of the exponential expansion:

e−θΔ=1−θΔ+O(Δ2). e^{-\theta\Delta}=1-\theta\Delta+O(\Delta^2).

The notation O(Δ2)O(\Delta^2) means that for fixed parameters, the magnitude of the omitted remainder is bounded by a constant times Δ2\Delta^2 for sufficiently small Δ\Delta. It identifies the order of the approximation error. Substituting into the conditional mean gives

mΔ(x)=x+θ(μ−x)Δ+O(Δ2). m_\Delta(x)=x+\theta(\mu-x)\Delta+O(\Delta^2).

Similarly,

vΔ=σ22θ(2θΔ−2θ2Δ2+O(Δ3))=σ2Δ−σ2θΔ2+O(Δ3). \begin{aligned} v_\Delta &=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta} \left(2\theta\Delta-2\theta^2\Delta^2+O(\Delta^3)\right)\\ &=\sigma^2\Delta-\sigma^2\theta\Delta^2+O(\Delta^3). \end{aligned}

The Euler approximation keeps only the leading mean change and leading variance: mean x+θ(μ−x)Δx+\theta(\mu-x)\Delta and variance σ2Δ\sigma^2\Delta. These are approximations to the exact transition, not its definition.

As Δ→∞\Delta\to\infty, the conditional mean tends to μ\mu and the conditional variance tends to qq. The process eventually loses predictive memory of the supplied current value, but not its randomness.

The half-life of a conditional deviation is the duration hh solving e−θh=1/2e^{-\theta h}=1/2. Taking logs gives −θh=−log2-\theta h=-\log 2, hence

h=log2θ. h=\frac{\log 2}{\theta}.

This measures halving of the forecast deviation, not a guaranteed time for a random sample path to reach a particular level.

If time is measured in days and XX in temperature units, θ\theta has units of 1/day1/\text{day} and σ\sigma has units of temperature divided by day\sqrt{\text{day}}. Then θΔ\theta\Delta is dimensionless, as required inside an exponential, and σ2/(2θ)\sigma^2/(2\theta) has units of squared temperature, as required for a variance.

Another useful limit holds μ,σ\mu,\sigma fixed and lets θ↓0\theta\downarrow0. Then mΔ(x)→xm_\Delta(x)\to x and vΔ→σ2Δv_\Delta\to\sigma^2\Delta: the model approaches scaled Brownian motion with no mean-reverting drift. The stationary variance diverges; at exactly θ=0\theta=0 there is no finite invariant Gaussian variance. The limiting behavior is consistent with losing the restoring force.

12.12 Recover AR(1) at observation times

For a fixed observation gap Δ\Delta, write Xi=XiΔX_i=X_{i\Delta}. The restart relation becomes

Xi=μ+ϕ(Xi−1−μ)+εi, X_i=\mu+\phi(X_{i-1}-\mu)+\varepsilon_i,

with

ϕ=e−θΔ,εi∼N(0,τ2),τ2=q(1−ϕ2). \phi=e^{-\theta\Delta}, \qquad \varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\tau^2), \qquad \tau^2=q(1-\phi^2).

The innovations are independent because they are deterministic-weight Brownian integrals over disjoint observation intervals. Thus a fixed-gap sampled OU process is an exact Gaussian AR(1), not just an approximation to one.

Conversely, given a fixed-gap AR(1) with 0<ϕ<10<\phi<1 and τ2>0\tau^2>0, take logs to recover

θ=−logϕΔ. \theta=-\frac{\log\phi}{\Delta}.

Rearranging τ2=[σ2/(2θ)](1−ϕ2)\tau^2=[\sigma^2/(2\theta)](1-\phi^2) then gives

σ2=2θτ21−ϕ2. \sigma^2=\frac{2\theta\tau^2}{1-\phi^2}.

The restriction 0<ϕ<10<\phi<1 matters. A stable AR(1) may have a negative coefficient, but no positive real θ\theta and positive gap produce a negative e−θΔe^{-\theta\Delta}. Such an AR fit is not a mean-reverting scalar OU model of the form used here.

With irregular gaps Δi\Delta_i, the same derivation gives ϕi=e−θΔi\phi_i=e^{-\theta\Delta_i} and τi2=q(1−ϕi2)\tau_i^2=q(1-\phi_i^2). The coefficients now change with the recorded gaps. This does not mean the underlying continuous-time OU mechanism changed; it means we observed that mechanism over different durations.

12.13 Two shorter transitions must agree with one longer transition

This consistency check is useful both conceptually and in code. Define ϕ(h)=e−θh\phi(h)=e^{-\theta h} and v(h)=q(1−ϕ(h)2)v(h)=q(1-\phi(h)^2). Starting from xx, transition for duration hh and then duration kk:

Xs+h=μ+ϕ(h)(x−μ)+ε1, X_{s+h}=\mu+\phi(h)(x-\mu)+\varepsilon_1,

Xs+h+k=μ+ϕ(k)(Xs+h−μ)+ε2=μ+ϕ(k)ϕ(h)(x−μ)+ϕ(k)ε1+ε2. \begin{aligned} X_{s+h+k} &=\mu+\phi(k)(X_{s+h}-\mu)+\varepsilon_2\\ &=\mu+\phi(k)\phi(h)(x-\mu)+\phi(k)\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2. \end{aligned}

The two innovations are independent, with variances v(h)v(h) and v(k)v(k). The retained deviation is ϕ(k)ϕ(h)=e−θ(h+k)=ϕ(h+k)\phi(k)\phi(h)=e^{-\theta(h+k)}=\phi(h+k). The combined variance is

ϕ(k)2v(h)+v(k)=q[ϕ(k)2(1−ϕ(h)2)+1−ϕ(k)2]=q[1−ϕ(k)2ϕ(h)2]=v(h+k). \begin{aligned} \phi(k)^2v(h)+v(k) &=q\left[\phi(k)^2(1-\phi(h)^2)+1-\phi(k)^2\right]\\ &=q\left[1-\phi(k)^2\phi(h)^2\right]\\ &=v(h+k). \end{aligned}

Thus the two-stage Gaussian transition has exactly the same mean and variance, and hence the same Gaussian distribution, as the single transition of duration h+kh+k. This is an explicit instance of the transition-composition property, also called the semigroup property.

12.14 A numerical transition with every quantity identified

Suppose the current observed value is x=29x=29, and use the candidate model parameters θ=1\theta=1, μ=25\mu=25, σ=2\sigma=2. For a gap Δ=0.5\Delta=0.5, the surviving fraction is

ϕ=e−0.5≈0.60653066. \phi=e^{-0.5}\approx0.60653066.

The current deviation from the target is 29−25=429-25=4, so the predicted next mean is

m=25+(0.60653066)(4)≈27.42612264. m=25+(0.60653066)(4)\approx27.42612264.

The stationary variance corresponding to these parameters is q=22/(2⋅1)=2q=2^2/(2\cdot1)=2. The conditional variance over this half-unit gap is smaller:

v=2(1−e−1)≈1.26424112. v=2(1-e^{-1})\approx1.26424112.

Its standard deviation is v≈1.12438\sqrt v\approx1.12438. Therefore the next value, conditional on the current reading and these parameters, has distribution approximately N(27.4261,1.2642)N(27.4261,1.2642). The prediction 27.4261 is not a guaranteed next value.

Gap Δ\Delta Retained fraction Conditional mean Conditional variance
0.10 0.9048 28.6193 0.3625
0.50 0.6065 27.4261 1.2642
1.00 0.3679 26.4715 1.7293
3.00 0.0498 25.1991 1.9950

The same starting value has different predictions and uncertainties at different horizons. This is why timestamps carry information about the return speed. The next chapter keeps that information inside every likelihood factor.

Source connection: the OU solution is treated in MIT Lecture 21, §1.2 and Särkkä and Solin, Examples 4.5 and 6.2. Here the solution is obtained through an ordinary equation for the noise-subtracted process, then verified directly; its distributions, stationarity and covariance are derived from the resulting formula.

13.1 What are the data, and what are the unknown parameters?

Suppose the quantity we are observing follows an OU model

dXt=θ(μ−Xt)dt+σdBt,θ>0,σ>0. dX_t=\theta(\mu-X_t)dt+\sigma dB_t, \qquad \theta>0,\quad\sigma>0.

Here μ\mu is the return level, θ\theta the return speed, and σ\sigma the continuous-time noise scale. The actual values of these parameters are unknown. We observe the process at times

t0<t1<⋯<tn t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n

and record numerical values

x0,x1,…,xn. x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n.

The data are the time–value pairs, not just the values without timestamps. Define each observed time gap by

Δi=ti−ti−1>0,i=1,…,n. \Delta_i=t_i-t_{i-1}>0,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.

There are n+1n+1 recorded values but only nn transitions between consecutive values. The gaps are known numbers calculated from the timestamps. We are not estimating them in this model. We are estimating

η=(θ,μ,σ). \eta=(\theta,\mu,\sigma).

For example, one small dataset is

Observation index Time tit_i Observed value xix_i Gap from previous observation
0 0.0 29.0 Not applicable
1 0.2 27.5 0.2
2 1.0 26.0 0.8
3 1.3 25.8 0.3

These four observations are a teaching example, not a claim that four readings provide reliable estimation of all OU parameters. Every candidate parameter triple will be evaluated on exactly this same dataset.

The maximization does not require us to know the true parameter before starting. As in the coin example, we ask what probability density the observed record would have under each hypothetical candidate. We then search for the candidate giving the largest likelihood, or equivalently the smallest negative log-likelihood.

13.2 The transition law needed for the likelihood

For a positive gap Δi\Delta_i, the OU solution has the restart form

Xti=μ+e−θΔi(Xti−1−μ)+εi, X_{t_i}=\mu+e^{-\theta\Delta_i}(X_{t_{i-1}}-\mu)+\varepsilon_i,

where the fresh noise term is

εi=σ∫ti−1tie−θ(ti−s)dBs. \varepsilon_i=\sigma\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}e^{-\theta(t_i-s)}\,dB_s.

The weight is deterministic. A weighted Brownian integral has mean zero and variance given by the integral of the squared weight, so

Var(εi)=σ2∫ti−1tie−2θ(ti−s)ds=σ22θ(1−e−2θΔi). \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i) &=\sigma^2\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}e^{-2\theta(t_i-s)}ds\\ &=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}(1-e^{-2\theta\Delta_i}). \end{aligned}

Different observation intervals use disjoint Brownian increments. Under the sampling assumptions below, their fresh noise terms are independent conditional on the recorded observation grid. Conditional on the current observed value, the next value therefore has the exact Gaussian distribution

Xti∣Xti−1=xi−1∼N(mi,vi), X_{t_i}\mid X_{t_{i-1}}=x_{i-1} \sim N(m_i,v_i),

with

ϕi=e−θΔi,mi=μ+ϕi(xi−1−μ),vi=σ22θ(1−ϕi2). \phi_i=e^{-\theta\Delta_i},\qquad m_i=\mu+\phi_i(x_{i-1}-\mu),\qquad v_i=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}(1-\phi_i^2).

The symbols ϕi,mi,vi\phi_i,m_i,v_i are functions calculated from a candidate parameter triple, the current observed value and the known gap. They are not extra free parameters to fit independently for every transition. All transitions share the same θ,μ,σ\theta,\mu,\sigma.

13.3 State the observation-time assumption before multiplying densities

The transition formula applies directly when observation times are fixed in advance. It also applies conditional on a realized random observation grid when the whole grid is independent of the entire OU path, including its initial value. In this second situation, first imagine drawing the observation times independently, then observing the process at those times.

Independence of the sampling design is not the same as the Markov property of the process. To see the distinction, suppose we decide to record the next observation when a continuous process first reaches a specified threshold aa. At that observation time, its recorded value is aa by construction. Conditional on this sampling rule and the hitting time, the observed endpoint is not an unrestricted Gaussian variable over the real line. The fact that the underlying process is Markov does not remove the information introduced by the observation rule.

The likelihood below therefore conditions on fixed or path-independent observation times. State-dependent observation schedules, noisy measurements and hidden states require the appropriate observation model. Also, if the distribution of the observation grid itself depends on unknown parameters, a full joint likelihood for times and values can contain additional parameter information in the time distribution. The conditional likelihood for values given times is a specifically chosen objective, not automatically the full likelihood of every possible data-collection scheme.

For the rest of this chapter, the initial value is either fixed or independent of future Brownian increments, the observed values have no additional measurement noise, and the observation grid satisfies the stated independence condition.

13.4 Derive the conditional likelihood rather than multiply marginals

The Gaussian transition density evaluated at the actual next observation is

gi(xi∣xi−1;η,Δi)=12πviexp[−(xi−mi)22vi]. g_i(x_i\mid x_{i-1};\eta,\Delta_i) =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v_i}} \exp\!\left[-\frac{(x_i-m_i)^2}{2v_i}\right].

The residual ri=xi−mir_i=x_i-m_i is the difference between the recorded value and this candidate model’s conditional mean. Different candidate parameters change both the predictions and their claimed variances.

Condition on the starting value x0x_0 and all observation times. The probability chain rule writes the joint density of the remaining observations as

Lc(η)=pη(x1∣x0,times)×pη(x2∣x0,x1,times)×⋯×pη(xn∣x0,…,xn−1,times). \begin{aligned} L_c(\eta) ={}&p_\eta(x_1\mid x_0,\text{times})\\ &\times p_\eta(x_2\mid x_0,x_1,\text{times})\times\cdots\\ &\times p_\eta(x_n\mid x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1},\text{times}). \end{aligned}

The OU Markov property shortens each conditional distribution to dependence on the immediately preceding value and the elapsed gap. Therefore

Lc(η)=∏i=1ngi(xi∣xi−1;η,Δi). \boxed{L_c(\eta)=\prod_{i=1}^n g_i(x_i\mid x_{i-1};\eta,\Delta_i).}

This is a product of conditional densities. The consecutive observed values are not independent. Multiplying their stationary marginal densities would describe a different statistical objective that discards the temporal dependence needed to estimate return speed properly.

Although we condition on x0x_0, we do not erase it from the calculation: it is used in m1m_1. Conditioning removes the need to assign a probability density to the supplied starting value. It does not remove the first transition from the dataset.

13.5 Take logs and keep the variance normalization

Take the logarithm of one transition factor:

loggi=log((2πvi)−1/2)+log(exp[−ri2/(2vi)])=−12log(2πvi)−ri22vi. \begin{aligned} \log g_i &=\log\left((2\pi v_i)^{-1/2}\right) +\log\left(\exp[-r_i^2/(2v_i)]\right)\\ &=-\frac12\log(2\pi v_i)-\frac{r_i^2}{2v_i}. \end{aligned}

The first equality uses the rule that the logarithm of a product is the sum of logarithms. The second uses log(ac)=cloga\log(a^c)=c\log a for positive aa, and log(ez)=z\log(e^z)=z.

Logs turn the full product into a sum. Negating it gives the negative log-likelihood, abbreviated NLL:

NLL(η)=12∑i=1n[log(2πvi)+(xi−mi)2vi]. \boxed{\operatorname{NLL}(\eta) =\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n\left[ \log(2\pi v_i)+\frac{(x_i-m_i)^2}{v_i}\right].}

Minimizing this is equivalent to maximizing the original likelihood because the log is increasing and negation reverses the ordering.

Both terms matter. The squared residual divided by viv_i measures the discrepancy relative to the uncertainty claimed by the candidate. The term logvi\log v_i accounts for the density becoming more spread out when variance increases. Removing that term would reward arbitrarily large variances: all residual penalties would approach zero as σ2\sigma^2 grew. The proper likelihood balances fit with the width of the prediction distribution.

The constant nlog(2π)/2n\log(2\pi)/2 can be omitted during optimization because it does not depend on any candidate parameter. But logvi\log v_i cannot generally be omitted: viv_i depends on θ\theta and σ\sigma.

13.6 Evaluate one candidate on a concrete dataset

Use the four readings from §13.1 and the candidate values θ=1\theta=1, μ=25\mu=25, σ=2\sigma=2. For the first gap Δ1=0.2\Delta_1=0.2,

ϕ1=e−0.2≈0.81873075, \phi_1=e^{-0.2}\approx0.81873075,

m1=25+0.81873075(29−25)≈28.27492301, m_1=25+0.81873075(29-25)\approx28.27492301,

and

v1=42(1−e−0.4)≈0.65935991. v_1=\frac{4}{2}(1-e^{-0.4})\approx0.65935991.

The actual next value is 27.5, so the residual is 27.5−28.27492301≈−0.7749230127.5-28.27492301\approx-0.77492301. The first negative-log contribution is

12[log(2π×0.65935991)+(−0.77492301)20.65935991]≈1.16606583. \frac12\left[\log(2\pi\times0.65935991) +\frac{(-0.77492301)^2}{0.65935991}\right] \approx1.16606583.

Now repeat the calculation for each actual transition. Importantly, the second prediction starts from the observed 27.5, not from the model’s previous predicted mean 28.2749. The likelihood conditions on the record that actually occurred.

Transition Gap Predicted mean mim_i Variance viv_i Residual rir_i NLL contribution

27.5→26.027.5\to26.0 0.8 26.123322 1.596207 −0.123322 1.157518
26.0→25.826.0\to25.8 0.3 25.740818 0.902377 0.059182 0.869518

Adding the three terms gives NLL(1,25,2)≈3.19310101\operatorname{NLL}(1,25,2)\approx3.19310101. The conditional likelihood density is consequently e−3.19310101≈0.04104439e^{-3.19310101}\approx0.04104439.

Keep μ=25\mu=25, σ=2\sigma=2 fixed and compare several candidate speeds on the same data:

Candidate θ\theta Conditional NLL Conditional likelihood density

Among these three candidates with the other two parameters fixed, θ=2\theta=2 has the largest likelihood. This comparison does not establish that 2 is the MLE over all positive speeds, much less the joint MLE over all three parameters. We have evaluated three points, not solved the entire optimization problem.

13.7 Why the parameters cannot simply be estimated separately

The conditional means depend on θ\theta and μ\mu, while the variances depend on θ\theta and σ\sigma. Changing the return speed therefore changes both the expected return toward the level and the amount of accumulated noise. This couples the fitting problem.

Nevertheless, we can simplify the optimization without pretending that the parameters are independent. Profiling means: fix one parameter temporarily, find the best values of the others at that fixed choice, and then compare those optimized scores across the first parameter.

For example, at candidate θ=1\theta=1, we can find the best μ\mu and σ\sigma conditional on that speed. At candidate θ=2\theta=2, we must generally find a different best μ\mu and σ\sigma. The result is a function of θ\theta alone, but it still incorporates the adjustment of the other parameters.

We will derive this reduction for the conditional likelihood with unrestricted real μ\mu and positive σ\sigma. A parameter-dependent initial-density factor, extra constraints, a prior, or a different observation model may change the formulas.

13.8 Rewrite the likelihood at a fixed candidate speed

Fix θ>0\theta>0 and calculate

ϕi=e−θΔi,bi=1−ϕi,ci=1−ϕi22θ,di=xi−ϕixi−1. \phi_i=e^{-\theta\Delta_i},\qquad b_i=1-\phi_i,\qquad c_i=\frac{1-\phi_i^2}{2\theta},\qquad d_i=x_i-\phi_i x_{i-1}.

All four quantities are now known for this fixed candidate θ\theta. Because every gap is positive and θ>0\theta>0, we have 0<ϕi<10<\phi_i<1, bi>0b_i>0, and ci>0c_i>0.

Expand the conditional mean:

mi=μ+ϕi(xi−1−μ)=ϕixi−1+(1−ϕi)μ. m_i=\mu+\phi_i(x_{i-1}-\mu) =\phi_i x_{i-1}+(1-\phi_i)\mu.

Therefore

xi−mi=di−biμ,vi=σ2ci. x_i-m_i=d_i-b_i\mu, \qquad v_i=\sigma^2c_i.

The likelihood has become a weighted fitting problem for the linear expression biμb_i\mu. Define

Sθ(μ)=∑i=1n(di−biμ)2ci. S_\theta(\mu)=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(d_i-b_i\mu)^2}{c_i}.

This is a weighted sum of squared residuals. The weights 1/ci1/c_i are positive and account for different amounts of transition noise at different gaps. Substituting into NLL gives

NLL(θ,μ,σ)=n2log(2π)+n2logσ2+12∑ilogci+Sθ(μ)2σ2. \operatorname{NLL}(\theta,\mu,\sigma) =\frac n2\log(2\pi) +\frac n2\log\sigma^2 +\frac12\sum_i\log c_i +\frac{S_\theta(\mu)}{2\sigma^2}.

At the fixed θ\theta, the cic_i are constants for the remaining optimization. The only dependence on μ\mu is through Sθ(μ)S_\theta(\mu).

13.9 Derive the profiled level estimate

Differentiate Sθ(μ)S_\theta(\mu) with respect to μ\mu. For one term, the chain rule gives

ddμ(di−biμ)2=2(di−biμ)(−bi). \frac{d}{d\mu}(d_i-b_i\mu)^2 =2(d_i-b_i\mu)(-b_i).

Hence

Sθ′(μ)=−2∑ibi(di−biμ)ci=−2∑ibidici+2μ∑ibi2ci. \begin{aligned} S_\theta'(\mu) &=-2\sum_i\frac{b_i(d_i-b_i\mu)}{c_i}\\ &=-2\sum_i\frac{b_i d_i}{c_i} +2\mu\sum_i\frac{b_i^2}{c_i}. \end{aligned}

Set this derivative equal to zero and move the first sum to the other side:

μ∑ibi2ci=∑ibidici. \mu\sum_i\frac{b_i^2}{c_i}=\sum_i\frac{b_i d_i}{c_i}.

Dividing by the positive denominator produces

μ̂(θ)=∑ibidi/ci∑ibi2/ci. \boxed{\widehat\mu(\theta) =\frac{\sum_i b_i d_i/c_i}{\sum_i b_i^2/c_i}.}

This is the unique minimum in μ\mu, not merely a stationary point, because

Sθ″(μ)=2∑ibi2ci>0. S_\theta''(\mu)=2\sum_i\frac{b_i^2}{c_i}>0.

The notation μ̂(θ)\widehat\mu(\theta) is important. It is a best-fitting level as a function of the speed being tried. It becomes part of a joint estimate only after a speed is selected. Also, this expression is not generally the arithmetic mean of the recorded xix_i: both the preceding values and gaps affect it.

Write

S(θ)=Sθ(μ̂(θ)) S(\theta)=S_\theta(\widehat\mu(\theta))

for the minimized weighted squared error at that speed.

13.10 Derive the profiled noise variance and the remaining objective

For fixed θ\theta and its best level, let s=σ2>0s=\sigma^2>0. The terms of NLL that depend on ss are

n2logs+S(θ)2s. \frac n2\log s+\frac{S(\theta)}{2s}.

Differentiate:

dds(n2logs+S2s)=n2s−S2s2=ns−S2s2. \frac{d}{ds}\left(\frac n2\log s+\frac{S}{2s}\right) =\frac{n}{2s}-\frac{S}{2s^2} =\frac{ns-S}{2s^2}.

When S>0S>0, the derivative is negative for s<S/ns<S/n, zero at s=S/ns=S/n, and positive for s>S/ns>S/n. Thus the unique minimum is

σ̂2(θ)=S(θ)n. \boxed{\widehat\sigma^2(\theta)=\frac{S(\theta)}{n}.}

The divisor is nn, the number of conditional transitions. This is a likelihood estimate, not an unbiasedness correction involving a regression degrees-of-freedom divisor.

At this estimate, S/(2σ̂2)=n/2S/(2\widehat\sigma^2)=n/2. Substitute back into the full expression:

NLLprofile(θ)=12{n[log(2π)+1+log(S(θ)n)]+∑ilogci}. \boxed{ \operatorname{NLL}_{\mathrm{profile}}(\theta) =\frac12\left\{ n\left[\log(2\pi)+1+\log\left(\frac{S(\theta)}n\right)\right] +\sum_i\log c_i \right\}.}

We have reduced a three-parameter problem to a one-dimensional numerical search over θ>0\theta>0. Once a minimizing speed is found, plug it into the derived formulas to obtain the associated level and noise estimates.

The case S(θ)=0S(\theta)=0 needs separate treatment. The fitted means then match every observed transition exactly at that candidate speed. As σ2↓0\sigma^2\downarrow0, the negative log-likelihood tends to −∞-\infty, so there is no ordinary positive interior noise-variance MLE at that speed. A numerical variance floor changes the permitted model and must not be hidden as though it were the unconstrained MLE.

Profiling also does not prove that the remaining objective has one global minimum or that its minimum lies in the interior. Boundaries and weak identification can still matter. A one-dimensional optimizer is a tool for finding the remaining optimum, not a proof that every run has found the correct global answer.

At θ=1\theta=1, the three observed gaps give approximately

b=(0.18126925,0.55067104,0.25918178), b=(0.18126925,\;0.55067104,\;0.25918178),

c=(0.16483998,0.39905174,0.22559418), c=(0.16483998,\;0.39905174,\;0.22559418),

and

d=(3.75680816,13.64345349,6.53872626). d=(3.75680816,\;13.64345349,\;6.53872626).

σ̂2(1)≈0.99068028,σ̂(1)≈0.99532923. \widehat\sigma^2(1)\approx0.99068028, \qquad \widehat\sigma(1)\approx0.99532923.
